title: Dwarka Expressway was sold as NCR’s Dubai. Buyers are flocking, roads & sewers missing
description: Thousands of families paid crores for homes along Dwarka Expressway, NCR's answer to Dubai's Sheikh Zayed Road. They got broken roads, open drains — ‘residents have to cross open fields to reach homes.’
author: Sagrika Kissu
content:
Gurugram: Prakhar Sahay fought for almost a decade to get the Dwarka Expressway built. He protested at Jantar Mantar in 2016 and lobbied endlessly so that his distant corner of Gurugram would finally be connected to Delhi. The expressway is here now, but Sahay is still fighting. This time it’s for the basic amenities residents were promised but never got.
In premium towers and affordable projects alike, thousands of families who have invested crores in homes along the Dwarka Expressway are grappling with broken approach roads, open drains, incomplete sewage networks and unreliable electricity. They live in apartments with clubhouses and tennis courts beside a Rs 9,000-crore expressway, but some still have to cross open fields to get home.
“I would always say that I wanted to see the Dwarka Expressway completed while I was still a father and not a grandfather. Now that it’s finally there, the surrounding infrastructure is nowhere to be seen,” said Sahay, convener of the Dwarka Expressway Gurugram Development Association.
Announced in 2006, the 29-kilometre Dwarka Expressway was billed as Delhi-NCR’s answer to Dubai’s Sheikh Zayed Road. Not just India’s first eight-lane elevated expressway, but the centre of a new oasis of urban planning that could give central Gurugram and Noida a run for their money.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the Gurugram stretch in March 2024 and the final Delhi section in August last year, though the building and buying boom had started well before that. Of the 42,816 units that were reportedly launched along the expressway between 2010 and 2024, 41,899 were sold in the same period. Today, about 115 housing projects are under construction. Sales of homes priced above Rs 10 crore have increased 22-fold in value to Rs 8,347 crore between 2024 and 2025. Real estate developers are marketing it as the new “power address”.
“Dwarka Expressway has been inspired by Dubai. Very soon, you will see towering skyscrapers lining the expressway just like Sheikh Zayed Road. The price rise after the launch of the expressway itself shows that it has become a power address,” said the sales manager of Roots Courtyard, which is selling plots starting at Rs 5 crore in a gated complex with amenities such as guards and EV chargers.
Connecting Mahipalpur in Delhi to Kherki Daula on the Manesar side of Gurugram, the road is an impressive sight, including its 3.6-km ‘musical’ underpass—a popular selfie spot with walls decorated with artwork representing different states. But the spectacle of the expressway ends where the neighbourhoods around it begin—whether it is luxury projects such as Tata La Vida or more modest developments such as ROF Alante.
The moment one turns off the Dwarka Expressway, the smooth, sweeping road gives way to broken access roads, clouds of dust and open drains. In newer sectors such as 99, 102, 104, 110 and 113, residents also contend with clogged stormwater lines and unreliable power. Many of the planned 24-metre and 30-metre internal roads remain unbuilt.
After repeated appeals to civic authorities went nowhere, the Dwarka Expressway Gurugram Development Association approached the Punjab and Haryana High Court last year over the missing roads. Haryana Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini promised a “permanent solution” in his March budget speech, but when the court asked for a timetable in September, the state still couldn’t say when it would finish acquiring the 1,157 acres needed for the 24-metre roads in Gurugram and Manesar.
Animals and drunkards enter the society at night. There was no STP until recently. My question is, how did the authorities issue the builder an occupancy certificate?
– Shivani Thusoo, ROF Alante resident
These sectors were meant to learn from the planning mistakes that have long plagued central Gurugram. Instead, they have inherited them in a more acute form.
“There are no internal roads, sewerage network or even drainage. Can you imagine, there are a few areas where residents have to cross open fields to reach their homes,” said Sahay. In his 40s now, he bought a 3BHK in Sidhartha Estella, Sector 103, in 2010, banking on the proposed expressway. A dispute with the builder has kept him in a rented flat nearby, at Rs 44,000 a month.
“It feels as though you must remain in complaint mode simply to secure the most basic amenities and necessities from the government,” he added.
Also Read: Inside Hyderabad’s housing glut. Unsold homes, skyscrapers without residents
A Rs 3-crore bubble
Tata La Vida in Sector 113 has all the trappings of a typical upscale Gurugram condominium: guarded gates, manicured gardens, a swimming pool, a well-equipped clubhouse, walking tracks and dedicated courts for tennis, badminton and basketball. Residents barely need to step out for daily necessities. Which is just as well, since they often don’t dare to.
Resident Kshitij Sharma paid Rs 3 crore for his apartment in 2024. The Dwarka Expressway was one of the clinchers. It promised easy access to Delhi and Gurugram, with IGI Airport just 15 minutes away. But the mess outside the gates has cast a pall, from piles of construction debris to the stagnant water lining both sides of the street all the way to the expressway.
“As soon as you step out of the society, the frustration really mounts. There is an open drain just 150 metres from our society. The approach road to the expressway is not built. And the sewage water lies stagnant on the roadside,” said 45-year-old Sharma, who works in the telecom sector. “I have everything inside my condominium, so unless it’s necessary, we don’t step out.”
As general secretary of the residents’ welfare association, Sharma spends much of his week shuttling between the offices of the Gurugram Metropolitan Development Authority (GMDA) and the Municipal Corporation of Gurugram (MCG), repeating the same demands for roads, drainage, sanitation and basic services.
“Each time, I am told that they are working on it. And somebody will come soon to fix the problems. But nobody comes. And then I will visit their office again with the same request,” he said.
At least three couples have sold their apartments in the past year. They were unable to put up with the day-to-day infrastructural and civic shortcomings. Several other owners are also actively discussing leaving Dwarka Expressway
– Kshitij Sharma, Tata La Vida resident
In a letter to the GMDA chief executive officer on 22 May, the La Vida Residents Welfare Association (LVRWA) wrote: “The storm water drain project in the area being managed by GMDA has seen no progress for months. The lack of a proper drainage route causes rainwater to seep into the ground, leading to dangerous levels of water ingress and seepage into society apartments.”
The letter also blamed non-functional streetlights on a pending electricity connection from GMDA. “Street light infrastructure has been in place for over two years, yet the road remains dark at night,” it said. Six months on, it still hasn’t been fixed.
Expressway, then potholes & open fields
When Shivani Thusoo moved into her new apartment in Sector 108 in 2025, the first thing she looked for was a road. There wasn’t one. Residents of neighbouring Nanakheri wouldn’t let the apartment owners use the village road. They told them to use the “government road”.
“But there was no government road,” said Thusoo, who moved here primarily because it offered both connectivity and affordability. With six towers and over 700 apartments, her society ROF Alante never had premium pretensions. But living here has turned out to be much more harrowing than Thusoo had expected.
The daily commute is like an obstacle course. Getting home from the expressway means driving nearly two kilometres on a bumpy, unpaved road through the neighbouring village of Nanakheri. Then comes a dusty path between fields. Only the last 100 metres are paved—a stretch built by the developer. Even this is an improvement. It took months of visits to government offices and an intervention by the local MLA before residents could use the village road.
“Outside our society, we have roads up to 100 metres. After that, it is all soil and potholes. I am tired of visiting government offices now, they never listen,” Thusoo said.
Last year, ROF Alante residents staged a heated protest outside the builder’s office in Sector 44, asking how the project had got a licence and an occupancy certificate without a proper approach road. The builder, in turn, blamed local landowners for digging up the road and blocking access to the society.
The road problem is not limited to Sector 108. Across the Dwarka Expressway, residents have protested time and again for 24-metre approach roads. Fixing accountability on this front has been a challenge.
Under the Gurgaon-Manesar Master Plan 2031, developers are responsible for the 24-metre internal roads and government agencies for the 60-metre roads between sectors. One reason for the mess is that each builder is responsible only for the stretch within its licensed area. So a road can be built up to the edge of one project and stop at the next plot, where the land hasn’t been acquired or ownership is in dispute.
The government has repeatedly acknowledged the problem but a solution has been slow to come. In August last year, Haryana Industries and Commerce Minister Rao Narbir Singh directed town planning officials to withhold occupancy certificates in Gurugram until builders constructed the approach roads they had promised. “Public convenience is paramount,” he said.
Then in his Budget speech, CM Saini referred to the road issue in Gurugram’s Sectors 58 to 115. Blaming previous governments for leaving land acquisition out of the development charges paid by builders, he said the state would now acquire the land and that “the expenditure incurred will be recovered from builders.”
Some movement at least has started. In September, Haryana set up a joint site inspection committee led by the zonal administrator of the Haryana Shehri Vikas Pradhikaran (HSVP), with officials from town planning, the city administration, land acquisition and urban estates. Of the roughly 1,157 acres needed for the missing roads, the state has zeroed in on about 38 acres in Sectors 58 to 67A and Sector 81 to acquire first. The committee will check land titles and submit a feasibility report to the HSVP’s chief administrator.
In Sector 109, Gaurav Prakash was among the early buyers along the corridor. He booked an apartment in 2010, when the expressway project was still getting repeatedly delayed by land acquisition, litigation and other issues. It was a leap of faith. According to him, the underlying issue is one of passing the buck. When residents asked officials for a proper approach road, he said, they were told it was the developer’s job.
I can’t lie to people and tell them that everything on the Dwarka Expressway is hunky-dory. I can only tell them the ground reality and let them make an informed decision
– Prakhar Sahay, real estate consultant
“But the developer had already built the stretch immediately outside their housing complex. The road beyond that is the government’s responsibility,” said Prakash.
The roads aren’t the only thing missing. Sewage tankers have become a familiar sight around societies along the Dwarka Expressway. With sewer lines incomplete or non-functional, they are the fallback for removing surplus treated effluent from in-house sewage treatment plants (STPs). But the solution is also a problem. Residents across societies say the tankers don’t take the waste to designated treatment plants, but instead dump it into open drains or vacant plots.
“Societies have their own STPs, but they cannot treat or reuse all the sewage. The surplus is meant to be taken to designated STPs, but it never reaches there,” said Prakash.
On 18 November, Municipal Corporation Manesar (MCM) Joint Commissioner Puneet Kumar caught two tankers dumping sewage in the open near the Holiday Inn by the expressway in Manesar and issued challans of Rs 50,000 each.
खुले में सीवरेज का गंदा पानी डालने वाले दो टैंकरों के 50-50 हजार रुपये के चालान
– संयुक्त आयुक्त @PuneetJ83054825 ने निरीक्षण के दौरान मौके पर किए चालान
– दोनों टैंकरों को जब्त करने के भी दिए आदेश@cmohry @ulbharyana @SwachhBharatGov @diprogurugram1 @DiprHaryana @DC_Gurugram pic.twitter.com/yPOxc3fH7N
— Municipal Corporation Manesar (@MCManesar) November 18, 2026
But many residents say they are yet to see their grievances addressed. Rajat Kumar, who lives in Sector 84, says he regularly files complaints on government portals with photographs of the tankers and the dumping.
“There is no answer or action,” he said.
Also Read: Gurugram, Noida are building for NRIs. Salaried class is trapped between dreams and means
Boom outside, bust inside
Soon after the Haryana stretch of the Dwarka Expressway opened in March 2024, prices along the corridor surged. A typical three-bedroom apartment went from around Rs 1.8 crore in 2022 to Rs 2.6 crore to Rs 4 crore by 2025.
The boom has attracted major developers, with new projects announced along the corridor, including Sobha City, M3M Capital, Adani The Marq and Roots Courtyard. But there are problems both outside and inside many of these complexes.
At ROF Alante, there is no proper boundary wall. A wire fence marks the edge, leaving the complex exposed to the fields beyond. Two massive diesel generators sit in the open beside the fence, their large exhaust pipes roaring. It would look like an industrial site were it not for the playground and small parking lot nearby.
Thusoo said the lack of a gate and boundary wall makes her worry for her family’s safety.
“Animals and drunkards enter the society at night. There was no STP until recently. My question is, how did the authorities issue the builder an occupancy certificate?” she said.
At Tata La Vida, about 600 apartments are occupied and only 70 are empty. But Kshitij Sharma says people are slowly trickling out and moving to Delhi and Noida.
“At least three couples have sold their apartments in the past year. They were unable to put up with the day-to-day infrastructural and civic shortcomings. Several other owners are also actively discussing leaving Dwarka Expressway,” said Sharma, with a sigh.
For Prakhar Sahay, the journey from fighting for the Dwarka Expressway to demanding basic amenities has reshaped his career. He moved from the corporate sector to real estate consultancy about five years ago.
“After a point, it feels like we should quit our jobs and spend all our time coordinating with the government to get the work done, simply because we bought a house here. That is why I decided to become a consultant,” said Sahay.
His conscience prevents him from endorsing his neighbourhood to would-be buyers.
“I can’t lie to people and tell them that everything on the Dwarka Expressway is hunky-dory. I can only tell them the ground reality and let them make an informed decision,” he said.
(Edited by Asavar Singh)

title: Dharmendra and the Deol dynasty dominance in Bollywood
description: Dharmendra made his debut in 1960 with Dil Bhi Tera Hum Bhi Tere, and went on to build a body of work that would define an era.
author: Triya Gulati
content:
Mumbai: When Neena Rao walked into Mumbai’s Breach Candy Hospital to see Dharmendra, it was Sunny Deol she ended up holding together. She felt him break down the moment they hugged.
“There, there, my brave Mr. Deol,” she told him, steadying the man India had spent decades watching play the toughest guy on screen. At that moment, even the ‘dhai kilo ka hath’ had felt powerless.
Rao spent nineteen years as Sunny’s manager before relocating to Germany in 2015. She has watched him carry the weight of? most people never see.
“He was like a rock for his family, as he has always been. But when Dharam ji was in hospital, he was broken from within. Sunny sir holds the family together. Family means absolutely everything to him,” she told ThePrint.
Three generations of Deols have made their mark on the film industry. Yet, ask anyone to name Bollywood’s great film dynasties, and the answer invariably comes down to the Kapoors or the Khans. The Deols rarely make the cut.
From Dharmendra’s debut in the 1960s, and Sunny Deol’s roar in Gadar, to Bobby Deol’s recent, hard-won second act, and a new generation in Karan and Rajveer Deol now stepping in front of the cameras. The Deols have survived Hindi cinema’s endless churn.
This isn’t a story about a famous surname pushing doors open in a closely-knit industry, though it may have done that too for the third generation. It’s the story of a family that kept reinventing what a Deol could do on screen — the romantic hero, the angry man, the vulnerable one, a patriot or a villain. However, off-screen, the Deols have all been grounded by a common thread: “a family man.”
“The film Apne actually mirrors the family dynamics of Deols. It’s a close knit family and they enjoy each other’s company. They don’t do things for the camera or Instagram. When the camera wasn’t rolling, the way they treated their father, the mutual love and respect Sunny and Bobby have for each other, it’s like a dream family,” Rao said.
The family and friends of Deols often say that they never promoted themselves, especially Sunny and Bobby. Both were media shy and focused largely on doing films, hoping that it would be just enough. But that has changed now.
“In 2023, when Sunny’s son (Karan Deol) got married, that was the first time they exposed themselves, they invited everyone. Cameras captured Sunny dancing. It was the first wedding of the Deols in so many years,” explained filmmaker Bablu Pachisiya. “It was followed by the release and the success party of Gadar 2.”
Pachisiya, who has produced Sunny’s films including Ziddi, Arjun Pandit and Farz, calls the family’s comeback as something totally unheard of. He is confident that the Deols are here to stay.
Debut of the Deols
Growing up in the 1970s, filmmaker Guddu Dhanoa lived in a one-room quarter in Delhi’s Sarojini Nagar. When Dharmendra, his cousin, came to visit him, Dhanoa remembered being bewildered. People gathered outside their house, climbing onto neighbouring buildings, just to catch a glimpse of him.
“Mai jab paida hua tha, tab voh insaan star tha (He was a star by the time I had been born). But we never felt that because he never had any starry tantrums. For us, he was always our Dharam ji. It’s only when we saw the crowds growing out of hand that we truly understood his stardom,” Dhanoa told ThePrint. “Showsha baazi and Dharam ji never co-existed.”
Through the 1970s and 1980s, Dharmendra built himself to become the industry’s most reliable heartthrob — the hero that every villain feared but every woman was infatuated with. Films like Phool Aur Patthar, Seeta Aur Geeta, Yaadon Ki Baaraat, Sholay, and Chupke Chupke earned him the moniker of the “He-Man of Hindi Cinema”.
That stardom, decades later, still had the power to stop a room. In 2018, Dharmendra flew to Dubai with sons Sunny and Bobby to promote Yamla Pagla Deewana Phir Se. What was meant to be a closed, invite-only luncheon at the Meydan Hotel, dissolved into pure chaos.
The moment the three Deols walked in, phones went up in the air, guests abandoned their food and it turned into a mad scramble for photos. Dharmendra had then told reporters, “It’s their love talking. Sometimes it’s like a flood and is a bit uncontrollable.”
But he left this superstardom at the doorstep, when he came home. It did not matter how he lived or what he wore or what he drove. Dhanoa insists none of it ever changed who Dharmendra was with the family. A trait his children have also inherited.
Dhanoa recalls that whenever relatives visited him in Mumbai during vacations and had to catch a train back to Delhi, Dharmendra insisted on personally dropping them to the station, no matter the hour.
“It was 5 in the morning, everyone would tell him it’s alright. But he was adamant to drop us off at the station. Stardom never got to his head. Never saw a change in him towards us, from my first memory to the last, he was the same,” said Dhanoa.
Dhanoa made his feature film directorial debut with the 1994 action-drama Elaan, starring Akshay Kumar and Madhoo. But, he started his career in the film industry as a producer, backing movies like Mera Lahoo (1987) and the major box-office hit Deewana (1992), which had become a launchpad for Shah Rukh Khan.
Senior film journalist Bharti Dubey, who has mapped the Deol family tree, explained that Satwant Kaur married Kewal Kishan Singh Deol, a schoolteacher, and together they had six children.
Their eldest, Santosh, passed away at just two years old. Dharmendra was their second child, followed by daughter Surindar, who also died young, from typhoid. The couple also had a son, Ajit, and daughters Harminder and Sudarshan.
Dubey revealed that Dharmendra was in Class 8 when the Partition tore India apart. He lost several childhood friends, who ended up migrating across the newly-created border. His father had hoped that Dharmendra would become a professor. But, Dharmendra, who was inspired by Dileep Kumar, applied for a Filmfare talent hunt contest in 1958. That decision set his entire Bollywood story in motion.
He made his debut in 1960 with Dil Bhi Tera Hum Bhi Tere, and went on to build a body of work that would define an era.
Dharmendra carried each of his highs and lows with a strange contentment. Not many know but Zanjeer, the film that would go on to make Amitabh Bachchan a superstar, was offered to Dharmendra first, Dhanao said. “He would say, if I had done Zanjeer, it would have been just another hit for me,” Dhanoa recalled.
Even Rajesh Khanna, who dominated the Hindi film industry on arrival, couldn’t dent Dharmendra’s standing. “When Rajesh Khanna came, he shook the industry. But there was one man who survived the craze of Khanna sahab — that was our Dharam ji,” the filmmaker added.
Long before any of that stardom, Dharmendra had already started a family. He married Prakash Kaur, from Bhanvora village, in an arranged marriage when he was just 19. By the time he entered films, he was already a father; his eldest, Sunny, was only a couple of years old. He and Prakash went on to have three more children, daughters Vijayta and Ajeeta, and son Bobby.
“Prakash bhabhi was very lucky for the family. His rise was phenomenal post-marriage. Dharam ji loved her and respected her a lot. She too held the family together, just the way Dharam ji would,” Dhanoa said.
Kaur has never spoken to the media in all these decades, maintaining a low profile even through Dharmendra’s second marriage to Hema Malini in 1980. Dharmendra and Hema had two daughters, Esha and Ahana Deol.
Dharmendra’s younger brother Ajit Singh Deol also entered the film industry and was known for films like Khhotte Sikkay, Meharbaani, and Barsaat — the 1995-film which was also Bobby Deol’s debut project. Ajit married Usha and the couple had three kids: Abhay, Ritu and Veerta. Ajit passed away in 2015.
The Deol dominance
Dhanoa, as was his routine, was getting ready to head to the sets of Ziddi when his phone rang. It was Sunny calling him home. The actor wanted Dhanoa to ride with him to the set, wanting to talk about a dance sequence he had been postponing for days.
“As soon as we sat in the car, Sunny went, ‘Aaj toh main tod dunga. Aisa dance karunga aap dekhna.’ When we reached the location, he backed out. He literally didn’t get down from the car,” Dhanoa recalled, laughing at the incident.
Eventually, choreographer Ganesh Acharya coaxed an awkward Sunny into a handful of for-the-sake steps on Mera Dil Le Gayi Oye Kammo Kidhar. Sunny, hands folded, barely moved. His co-star Raveena Tandon refused to even call it dancing.
“Sunny ko dance karana bahut mushkil tha (It was very tough to get Sunny to dance),” Dhanoa said.
Rao describes Sunny in four words: “reserved, humble, workaholic and a big foodie.”
Their 19-year-long run together, though, had a rocky start. For the first six months, Sunny couldn’t even remember her name.
“He took his time adjusting to me and then we became family,” Rao said, recalling how he stood by her through one of her hardest stretches, her mother’s knee surgery. “He got the best doctor in Breach Candy and ensured the best treatment.” Rao turned out to be lucky for Sunny in more ways than one. During their alliance, he delivered back-to-back hits with Jeet, Ghatak, Border, Ajay and Ziddi. But, Gadar: Ek Prem Katha broke all records of stardom.
She remembers watching an early preview of Gadar, with Sunny. The film didn’t even have an ending yet. Still, Sunny was convinced that the film would work.
“He told me, ‘this film has a soul and it will be a hit’,” Rao said. “However, we didn’t anticipate that it would become a phenomenon.”
When she caught an early show at Ishaan theatre in Vile Parle, she couldn’t hear a single line of dialogue over the crowd’s cheering. “The audience was hooting throughout. I just heard the people cheering for two hours,” she said.
When theatres in Punjab started adding early-morning shows, just to keep up with the demand, Rao said, they realised Gadar wasn’t just a hit, it was a blockbuster.
“At that time, early morning shows were unheard of, that’s why it was definitely a parameter,” Rao said. “It was like, Sunny could do no wrong.”
Then the first shoe dropped.
After the release of Indian in October that year, Sunny slid into a bad patch that stretched over two decades. His solo box-office pull thinned out into a string of commercial misses.
“He wasn’t depressed. He would take 1-2 days to process the setback but then he diverted his attention to production. He is a great actor, but he is also a filmmaker within himself,” Rao said, recalling how the actor would show up even on weekends and holidays.
Bobby’s own dry spell arrived a little later, in the late 2000s and early 2010s, after a strong run through the late 1990s and early 2000s with films like Barsaat (1995), Gupt (1997), Soldier (1998), and Humraaz (2002).
“The good scripts simply stopped landing on the desks,” said Rao, who describes Bobby as someone who is “more expressive, who can’t hide emotions.”
That said, not every Deol managed to attract the same stardom. Abhay Deol, Dharmendra’s nephew, entered the industry in 2005 with Socha Na Tha and spent the years after deliberately swimming against the current, picking off-kilter, low-budget roles in films like Manorama Six Feet Under, Oye Lucky! Lucky Oye!, and Dev D over the mainstream vehicles his cousins were built for.
“I feel my advantage of coming from a film family is that having seen the fame up close, having seen the industry and how it works, I was not enamoured by fame,” he once said. “I wasn’t looking to be a star, I just happened to love acting, I was a reluctant actor.”
Abhay has also been openly skeptical of the industry’s reward system, once commenting, after being passed over for a Filmfare nomination for Dev D: “It was a family fare. If you are part of the family, then you will get it.”
The Deol family
The daughters of the family charted their own paths but weren’t as lucky as their half-brothers.
Esha Deol stepped into films in the early 2000s with roles in Dhoom, Kaal and No Entry, before gradually stepping back from acting in favour of family life. She made a comeback in 2022 with the psychological thriller series Rudra: The Edge of Darkness but it was no more than a blip in her career.
Esha’s younger sister, Ahana, took a different route from the beginning. She never seriously pursued films at all.
Over the years, time and again, news surfaced that the two families of Dharmendra had clashes and fallouts. But, Rao set the record straight once and for all.
“Bobby and Sunny have a great relationship with their half-sisters. People lie when they say that the two families and siblings have animosity,” she said.
Just like the Deols, their story was never just about box office hits or comebacks — because underneath all of it, the Deols were rooted in their family.
“Dharmendra has 13 grandchildren,” Dubey revealed.
Sunny and his wife Pooja have two sons, Karan and Rajveer. Dharmendra and Prakash’s second-born daughter, Vijayta, married Vivek Gill, and the couple has two children, Prerna and Sahil. Her sister Ajeeta, who lives in the USA, also has two kids of her own. Bobby, who was born Vijay Singh Deol, has two children with his wife, Tanya Ahuja. Esha has two daughters from her marriage to businessman Bharat Takhtani, while Ahana, also married to a businessman, Vaibhav Vohra, has three children: a son, Darien, and twin daughters, Adea and Astraia.
Comeback of the Deols
Pachisiya, who is also a family friend of the Deols, revealed that the decade-long slump was financially draining for the family. The films they bankrolled too didn’t do great business.
“Paise ka dikkat aa gaya tha,” Pachisiya said.
The stars of the Deol family re-aligned in 2020. When Bobby signed Class of 83 and Aashram within a week of each other, he hadn’t told his parents or Sunny. Both films, particularly Aashram, broke his boyish, romantic image the industry had boxed him into for decades.
“OTT completely changed my life. Class of 83 was the beginning, but Ashram changed my entire life,” Bobby later said in an interview.
By the time Animal arrived in 2023, casting him as a terrifying antagonist, Bobby as Nirmal Baba had become, in Sunny’s own words, something close to “the Gadar of the OTT platform.”
Bobby’s entry song Jamal Kudu became a social media phenomenon. It was like Bobby was getting his long pending due from the industry. However, it was Sunny’s Gadar 2 which unexpectedly rewrote box office records.
The limited 2023 4K re-release of Gadar: Ek Prem Katha minted approximately Rs 7.78 crore globally, while its sequel, Gadar 2, grossed an astronomical Rs 691.08 crore worldwide during its theatrical run.
“I was quite stressed over the period of time and when this film hit the cinema halls, I don’t know why it felt like God came inside me. I was crying and laughing all night and evening,” he said, describing the release weekend.
The success party of Gadar 2 saw the who’s and who of Bollywood including Shah Rukh Khan, Salman Khan and Aamir Khan.
For an industry that had, for years, treated both brothers as relics of a different Bollywood, 2023 became the year the Deol name roared back.
Pachisiya also points out that while most actors of Sunny’s age have settled into character roles, he is still headlining, playing the lead in Gadar 2 and Border 2, as well as upcoming projects like Batwara and Ramayana, where he plays the role of Hanuman.
The next-gen Deols
The third generation of the Deol clan hasn’t quite made a mark yet. Their debuts happened and were forgotten quickly.
Karan, Sunny’s elder son, made his lead debut in 2019 with Pal Pal Dil Ke Paas, a romantic drama that Sunny directed, its title borrowed from one of Dharmendra’s popular songs. Sunny had called it a full-circle moment.
“My father launched me and now I am launching my son. Karan is extremely passionate about his acting career and I am sure he will do everyone proud,” he said. But, the film opened to a different reality.
It earned roughly Rs 8 crore against a production budget several times that, and the reviews were brutal. Karan did receive some shreds of credit for his acting even though the film collapsed. However, the title track, ironically, went on to rack up over 200 million YouTube views, outliving the movie in public memory.
Karan later admitted the experience had rattled him, but insisted he wouldn’t let it derail him: “Can’t let anything put me down.”
Rajveer’s debut, four years later, followed an almost identical arc. He entered Bollywood in 2023 with Dono, a Rajshri Productions coming-of-age love story that also marked director Avnish Barjatya’s debut. His father Sooraj Barjatya once launched Salman Khan with Maine Pyar Kiya. But, the magic didn’t repeat.
Dono opened even softer than his brother’s debut had. It reportedly collected around Rs 35 lakh on its first day, a crore less than what Pal Pal Dil Ke Paas had managed in its own opening.
Dharmendra had introduced Rajveer to the public. He said, “Introducing my grandson Rajveer Deol to the world of cinema… I humbly request you all to shower the same love and affection on both the kids as you have on me.”
While Rao is biased towards the boys, Pachisiya admits that their debut films weren’t great.
“The truth is when his sons made their respective debut, Sunny wasn’t a superstar. He spent so much money and it bombed. Jab samay nhi chalta, toh aap kuch sahi karo, kaam nhi hoga (When the time is not right, nothing will work)” the producer explained.
Karan starred with his father in Rajkumar Santoshi’s Batwara 1947, which released on 14 August, but that too struggled on the box office.
The next generation of Deols have a long way to go to earn a place for themselves in the industry. That said, who knows when they find their Gadar or Ashram moment.
(Edited by Aakriti Handa)

title: ECI’s Bengal SIR Dashboard Used Hard-Coded Numbers Instead of Live Data, Code Analysis Finds - The Wire
description: Certain numbers – like how many Bengal voters were marked for ‘logical discrepancies’ – appear to be hard-coded into the dashboard, instead of using a dynamic code that would change with updates.
author: Aparna Bhattacharya
content: Kolkata: Some of the most important West Bengal numbers on the Election Commission’s portal appear to be typed straight into the portal’s code, rather than a dynamic figure that changes with the count.That is the finding of an independent analysis of ECINet, the Commission’s online system for managing electoral rolls, which officers, observers and the Commission itself use to track the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls.The Wire began looking into ECINet’s code after a tip-off. It then asked three senior computer scientists and a cybersecurity expert, each with decades of experience in the field, to examine the findings independently. All of them do not want to be named.The code was publicly available until November 23 – when the code page started redirecting to an ECI log in page. This change occurred two days after The Wire reached out to the ECI with queries about the code.What was examinedThe analysis examined the code of the ECINet website itself, as last accessed on November 18. The server’s own records show that code was last changed on October 16, 2026.A portal like ECINet works in two parts. The Commission’s database stores the real figures: how many voters were flagged, how many notices went out, how many hearings were held. Each time an official opens the dashboard, the screen asks the database for the latest figures and shows whatever comes back. When the data changes, the screen changes with it.A number typed into the code skips that step. Instead of asking the database, the programmer writes the figure directly into the instructions for the screen, and the screen shows that figure every time, whatever the database holds. Programmers call this hard-coding. It is sometimes used while a system is being built or tested, but a live dashboard that officials rely on is expected to show the changing data, not a fixed number.Think of a scoreboard at a cricket ground. It is fed by the scorers, and it is supposed to change with every run. Imagine one where, for one team only, the score has been painted on. The match goes on, runs are scored and wickets fall, but the board shows the same number. The players, the umpires and the crowd all look at it, and nothing on the board tells them it has stopped following the game.ECINet is that scoreboard for the SIR. Its dashboards are meant to show what the Commission’s database holds, and the officers, observers and courts following the revision rely on them. The analysis found that for West Bengal, some of those figures are painted on. They are written into the portal’s code, so they stay the same whatever happens to the real count unless the portal’s developers change that code, and on the screen they look exactly like live figures.A number that does not changeECINet has a dashboard that shows how many voters in each state were flagged for “logical discrepancies”, the mismatches in names, ages and family details that sent voters to hearings during the SIR.For every state, the dashboard shows the figure from the Commission’s database. Except one. When West Bengal is chosen, the code shows 94,49,132, whatever the database says.The code that does this is public. It sits in a file the portal sends to every visitor’s browser, ecinet.eci.gov.in/static/js/9226.e7540559.chunk.js. The line reads:children: [“Electors with Discrepancies – “,(0,A.Cc)(“West Bengal”==Tl&&bo ? 9449132 : mo?.anomalyCount)]Screenshot of the code as accessed on November 18, 2016.It is a simple either-or instruction.If the state is West Bengal and the statewide view is selected, the screen shows the fixed number 94,49,132, written in the code as 9449132. Otherwise, it shows “anomalyCount”, the figure the portal receives from the Commission’s database. For all other states, the statewide total of electors with discrepancies comes from the data. For West Bengal, it comes from the code.The number 94,49,132 is the official count of electors in West Bengal whose entries were flagged for logical discrepancies during the Election Commission’s verification drive, the voters who were then called to prove their place on the roll.The code cannot say why. That count was published in February, so the code may hold a frozen copy of it. It may be a workaround for a problem with the server’s own count. Or it may be something else. The only way to know is to compare it with what the Commission’s database actually returns, which needs authorised access. What the code does show is that if the real number changed after February, as cases were reviewed, flagged again or sent to judges, anyone looking at the dashboard would not see the change.Hearings counted from a fixed figureA second dashboard tracks the notices sent to voters and the hearings held. For West Bengal, the code sets the number of notices to 1,51,92,735, and then works out the number of hearings from that fixed figure.In other words, the screen’s count of hearings in Bengal depends partly on a number written into the code, not only on what the database records. West Bengal is the only state whose notices and hearings figures depend on a number in the code. In the drill-down views, district and below, Bengal’s figures come from the database too. The only other figure the code replaces on this dashboard is Tamil Nadu’s count of cases “found not OK”.That figure is close to, but not identical to, the 1,51,92,634 hearing cases recorded in the Commission’s own ERONET status report from the deadline night of February 21. The hearing stage is where The Wire’s reporting has found the SIR’s official figures repeatedly failing to add up. On the Commission’s own records, electoral registration officers had decided 94% of hearing cases by the deadline, yet 60 lakh voters were still sent to judges a week later.The rules that flagged voters, written into a screenThe West Bengal discrepancy dashboard also lists the rules used to flag voters. They are typed directly into it:the voter’s parent is linked to six or more children on the roll (“Progeny >= 6”);the father’s name does not match;a parent and child are less than 15 years apart in age, or more than 50;a grandparent and grandchild are less than 40 years apart.These are the “logical discrepancies” that sent millions of Bengal voters to hearings, and many of them on to judges. In one case The Wire has seen on the portal, a woman in Deganga was flagged because six other voters had named the same man as their father.Rules that decide whether a citizen is called to prove their place on the roll would normally be set out in a published order, and kept in settings that officials control and auditors can check. Here the list appears in the code of a single screen, which only the portal’s developers can change, and which officials and auditors cannot easily see or review.‘Backup’ turnout figures never updatedThe analysis also found a backup screen for voter turnout. If the live turnout feed fails, it shows fixed figures for West Bengal – 2,84,19,840 votes out of 3,60,77,304 electors, a turnout of 78.77%, with a “last update” of April 11, 2026. The state assembly election was held in two phases – April 23 and April 29 (both after April 11, when the 78.77% backup number was put in).The total electors figure on the screen is not a placeholder. It matches, to the last digit, the official number of electors eligible to vote in the first phase of polling. After scrutiny of the Phase 1 vote, the Commission put that number at 3,60,77,304On April 20, the Commission had announced 3,60,77,171 Phase 1 electors. On the eve of polling, the SIR tribunals restored a further 139 voters, and eight names earlier added by judicial officers were removed. The final number was settled only around polling day on April 23. So the screen holds a figure from after the date it claims as its last update. The code was evidently changed after April 11, but the date in the code was not.The turnout on the screen, 78.77%, or 2,84,19,840 votes, is not the final figure of 93.19%, or 3,36,20,168 votes.However, turnout on the screen is not invented either. It is the turnout recorded at 3 pm on polling day. According to the Commission’s own hour-by-hour figures for April 23, seen by The Wire, Phase 1 turnout stood at 78.77% at 3 pm, the same figure fixed in the code. The screen also holds turnout percentages for the 16 districts that voted in the first phase, and these match the same 3 pm figures: 79.88% for Bankura, 80.22% for Birbhum and 77.53% for Alipurduar. Beside each, the code records zero voters – indicating that the code was not updated completely and only the turnout percentages were hard-coded in the backup.Time stamps hidden in the code show when these snapshots were taken: 3:33 pm and 5:33 pm on April 23. They appear to have been copied from the live turnout feed on polling day and saved into the portal, where they were still sitting on October 16.There is no evidence that this backup screen was ever shown to anyone. But it is still significant that the backup was never updated, as this is an important official historical record that may have been required at any moment. Instead, the ECI appears not to have ensured that these numbers were updated.If the backup was used, the live screen would show the figures with their poll date and the note “As at 03:00 PM”, so the label itself is accurate. The problem is what it would show at any other time. If the live feed failed later that evening, the screen would present the 3 pm figures as the latest turnout, with nothing to tell officials that they were looking at saved numbers rather than live ones. If it failed on April 29, the second day of polling, the screen would show the first phase’s figures instead, marked only with the earlier poll date. The code holds no figures from April 29, which suggests the snapshots were taken once, on April 23, and not updated after that.Screenshot of the code as accessed on November 18, 2016.Why it mattersOn a screen, a number typed into the code looks exactly like one drawn from live data. The officers, observers and courts relying on ECINET to follow the SIR in Bengal would have no way to tell the two apart.That matters in a revision where the Commission’s public figures have repeatedly not matched its own records. When the roll was frozen in April, 22,163 cases were described publicly as decided and awaiting only an e-signature. The Commission’s own report records the same 22,163 as not decided before the assembly election. The office of the Chief Electoral Officer now says 5,819 cases remain pending across the state. The electoral rolls of just 11 Murshidabad constituencies record 29,347 voters still under adjudication.Based on publicly available filesThis analysis is based only on the files the portal sends to browsers, which are publicly available. It could not see what the Commission’s servers hold or return, and it does not show what was actually done with the portal. Why the fixed values are there, whether as test data left behind, a snapshot frozen in place or a deliberate substitution, cannot be told from the code.The analysis found no fields for religion, caste or community anywhere in the files, and no feature that deletes voters automatically at this particular stage. Every removal needs an officer to act. Its authors withdrew or narrowed 12 of their own earlier claims after checking them against the code.Questions for the CommissionThe Wire has asked the Election Commission why these West Bengal figures are fixed in the portal’s code, what the true counts in its database are, which order sets out the rules used to flag voters, and why a backup turnout screen holds figures that weren’t updated. This report will be updated when the Commission responds.Two days after The Wire sent its questions to the Commission on Saturday, November 21, 2026, public access to ECINet’s code was restricted. Visitors trying to open the portal’s code files are now redirected to ECINet’s login page, which asks for a user ID, a captcha and a one-time password before anything can be seen. The Commission has not said whether the change was connected to The Wire’s questions.ECINet was redeployed on November 23. The server records a new version of the site published at 7:35 pm IST that day. The portal now loads a new main file, and its list of files has changed.The Wire has preserved a complete copy of the code as on November 18, with a digital fingerprint for each file.With inputs from The Wire Staff.For our full coverage on the SIR and the issues it has brought to citizens, click here.

title: US Proposes Up to 25% Tariff on India Citing ‘Excess Manufacturing Capacity’ - The Wire
description: However, Washington said it will consider lowering the new tariff to 17% if the two sides can reach a trade deal.
author: The Wire Staff
content: New Delhi: Washington proposed a new tariff of up to 25% on Indian goods on Wednesday (November 25) in response to what it called India’s unfair excess manufacturing capacity. However, it said it will consider lowering the levy to 17% if the two sides reach a trade agreement.The commerce and industry ministry responded by reiterating that India does not have a structural excess capacity in any sector. New Delhi believes that all trade-related concerns ought to be addressed within the framework of the two sides’ trade deal talks, it said.In a press release on Wednesday evening Indian time, the office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced its recommendations pursuant to an investigation launched in March into the excess manufacturing capacity and production of over a dozen economies. At up to 25%, India faces the highest base tariff, second only to Vietnam’s 35%.However, the USTR will consider lowering India’s proposed tariff to 17% if it reaches a trade deal with the US – talks on which began in February 2025 but have since stalled – that address its excess capacity concerns, it said.Japan, South Korea and the European Union had a 15% tariff recommended on their goods, while a levy of up to 18% was proposed on products coming from Bangladesh, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand. All of these economies have already signed trade deals with the Trump administration, which has aggressively employed tariffs since assuming power early last year.Singapore faces a duty of up to 20% that could halve to 10% if it strikes a trade deal with the US. On the other hand, the USTR said it would consider reducing Vietnam’s proposed 35% tariff to 20% in the event that an agreement is reached. China too had a levy of up to 20% recommended on a section of its goods.India’s proposed tariff of up to 25%, which would be levied under section 301 of America’s Trade Act, will not apply to certain exempted goods or on top of the 10% tariff that Washington announced earlier this year under the same section citing a separate investigation. It will also not stack on to the US’s separate aluminium and steel tariffs.Releasing a 189-page report on its findings on India, the USTR cited the country’s above-average share of manufacturing in GDP, below-average share of consumption, and “large and persistent trade surpluses” with America as among its reasons for recommending the up-to-25% tariff.India, it went on to say, “enhances its own growth in capacity, production and exports without commensurately seeking growth in its own demand, consumption or imports”. Its practices “burden or restrict US commerce by harming the US economy through lost exports, persistent trade deficits and a diminished manufacturing sector”, the USTR alleged.New Delhi said it has taken note of the USTR’s findings and that it is examining them. “India engaged constructively throughout this investigation,” the commerce ministry said, adding that after Washington began its proceedings in March it had argued that India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector.“It has been India’s position that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of these negotiations. Government of India remains committed to working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement, as announced on February 2, 2026 and in accordance with the Joint Statement issued on February 7, 2026,” it continued.The White House will next seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing January 25, suggesting the duties won’t take effect until February or March.As part of its tariff policies, the Trump administration in April 2025 unveiled ‘reciprocal’ tariffs on nearly all of the US’s trading partners, including a levy of around 25% on India, which kicked in later that year. Then, it stacked a further 25% tariff on Indian goods in response to Indian refiners’ sustained purchases of Russian oil, straining bilateral ties.US President Donald Trump went on to announce in February of this year that his administration would lower the unprecedented 50% tariff to 18% as part of an understanding towards a trade deal. India would slash all tariff and non-tariff barriers on American goods, he had claimed.Days later, the Supreme Court in Washington D.C. struck down the Trump administration’s ‘reciprocal’ tariff regime, following which a temporary 10% levy went into effect against many countries, including India.Then, in March, the USTR announced its investigations into forced labour and excess capacity. When the temporary 10% tariff expired in July this year, Washington levied an identical duty on India citing the findings of its forced labour investigation. At that time, New Delhi had said this would only apply to 55% of its exports, with generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones being among the products that continued to enjoy no duties.Two months later, the US federal legislature passed the Lindsey Graham Act that authorises Trump to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian energy. India falls into that category, having become the biggest importer of seaborne Russian crude oil. Trump has put the legislation on hold for now.While sweeping, Wednesday’s tariffs largely replace those first imposed last April and should have a modest impact on inflation and growth, economists said.At the same time, the announcement demonstrates the Trump administration’s willingness to continue imposing tariffs even after voters in this month’s midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats. About two-thirds of voters said that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, according to the AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.With inputs from AP.

title: A Thumbs Up to the BJP's Own 'Dimagi Naxal' - The Wire
description: The defence of Sonia Gandhi's memoir against vandalism is a reminder that defending freedom of expression need not depend on ideological agreement.
author: Badri Raina
content: In her best-selling memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, Congress leader Sonia Gandhi has mentioned the well-known fact from India’s anti-colonial freedom struggle that Vinayak Damodar Savarkar wrote repeatedly from the Cellular Jail, seeking a pardon from his oppressors.Understandably, this fact remains unpalatable to the right-wing, which often cannily tries to wish it away as a measure recommended to Savarkar by M.K. Gandhi, or interprets it as yet another astute political move by the Hindutva leader, thereby making his subsequent career in consolidating Hindu cultural nationalism possible.Thus it came to pass a few days ago that such offending pages were torn from Gandhi’s book by some members of the Shiv Sena in Maharashtra.But lo and behold, a Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) minister in the right-wing Maharashtra Cabinet, one Ashish Shelar, came forth to object to the vandalism visited upon the book.He did not necessarily concur with what she has written. Instead, his objection rested on the admirably principled ground that such vandalism, practised on books that we do not like, bespeaks barbarism rather than democratic or civilisational forbearance towards facts and ideas antithetical to some sections of society.Also read: From ‘Vande Mataram’ to ‘Dimagi Naxal’: The BJP’s Political Tests Have Nothing to Do With Actual PatriotismSo we say, three thumbs up to this minister, clearly and demonstrably a “Dimagi Naxal” within the nationalist pantheon, who chooses to retain a questioning mind when it comes to the plurality of positions in social and intellectual life.Shri Shelar’s intervention in the fraught matter helps to remind us that not all forms of conservative politics have historically been monologic or fascistic, but that many worthwhile contributions to the evolution of democratic ideas and practices can be attributed worldwide to groups and individuals who, however wedded to their often reactionary thought processes, stopped short of claiming suzerainty over values for themselves.The interesting speculation is how far this minister’s example may travel in ameliorating the intolerance of the right-wing towards facts and ideas they do not like, however germane or valid their substance.To employ a non sequitur, were those who regard themselves as god’s own chosen variety of the human species to have their entire moral and intellectual universe confined to just an edict or two, a bookless universe might well be born. In it, only a handful of scriptures, at war with each other, might constitute the library of humankind – a prospect, incidentally, to which more than one modern leader of standing seems now well and truly wedded.Shelar’s questioning reminds us that there were once leaders like Atal Bihari Vajpayee, who loved the rich archive of Urdu poetry as much as the current crop of right-wing leaders hate it, and do everything to make it disappear.Also read: Let’s Draw the Line at Vajpayee’s VerseThe regrettable and hurtful impoverishment of India’s rich legacies, which the cyclopes in charge of national destiny now seek to aggravate, could well be reversed should more and more members of the empowered right-wing see the beauty and necessity of Shelar’s courageous questioning – and allow the country’s cultural and ideational pluralities to live out their conjoint splendours in an atmosphere of free expression and enquiry rather than subject them to the proverbial jackboot of top-down diktat.Most especially, Shelar’s objection to the vandalism of books on account of their inconvenient contents may be extended to reversing the blight that has come to visit educational curricula, wherein not only are “other” points of view ejected from school, college and university courses, but entire books are removed from libraries and bookshops.We do not know if Shelar has any liking for the first Indian prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, but to the extent that he reminds us of that open-minded stalwart, we see hope that time may overtake the right-wing’s revanchist historical and ideational preferences, allowing the emergence of a social, cultural and intellectual order that is free of the pollution of diktat.“Dimagi” Naxalism may not be such an odious thing after all.Badri Raina taught at Delhi University.

title: Bomba, Legends of Delhi ft. Aslam Chicken, So Tammy’s Join Time Out Market Delhi
description: The new additions bring a homegrown pizzeria, an Old Delhi food institution and a chef-led Mexican restaurant to the Market’s growing selection of culinary talent.
author: The Quint
content:
Note: Quint Digital Limited (QDL) is bringing the first Time Out Market to India, with a flagship location at Worldmark Aerocity, Delhi. The launch is part of QDL’s franchise agreement with Time Out Group plc.
Time Out Market Delhi, the food and cultural destination opening in December 2026 at 5 Worldmark, Aerocity, has announced three new additions to its culinary line-up: Bomba, Legends of Delhi featuring Aslam Chicken, and So Tammy’s. The announcement marks another step towards the opening of India’s first Time Out Market, bringing together established neighbourhood favourites and contemporary dining concepts in a new setting.
The latest additions also introduce new ways to experience the city's food culture, from dishes created exclusively for the Market to a rotating platform that will showcase Old Delhi’s iconic eateries and introduce their culinary traditions to a wider audience.
Spanning approximately 25,000 sq. ft., Time Out Market Delhi will feature 11 kitchens, two full-service bars and a live performance stage, with seating for around 500 guests.
Bomba
Bomba, the homegrown favourite known for its thin-crust pizzas and pasta, brings a creative take on familiar comfort food. For Time Out Market Delhi, the brand will introduce new dishes alongside its signature offerings, which include pastas, tapas-style plates and a stuffed pull-apart garlic bread skillet.
“Bomba has always been about bringing people together over food that is familiar, fun and full of flavour. Being part of Time Out Market Delhi gives us an opportunity to take the brand to a wider audience while introducing dishes created especially for the Market. From our signature thin-crust pizzas to our new pastas, we want guests to discover something they love, try something different and enjoy food in a setting that brings people together. It is exciting to be part of a space that celebrates the diversity and evolving character of Delhi’s food scene,” says Chef Alisha Mehra, Founder, Bomba.
Legends of Delhi featuring Aslam Chicken
Curated in association with Anubhav Sapra, Founder of Delhi Food Walks, Legends of Delhi is a rotating culinary concept that will bring some of the city’s oldest, iconic eateries to Time Out Market Delhi. This first-of-its-kind initiative will spotlight the capital’s rich food heritage while giving established local vendors a platform to showcase their specialities to new audiences in a global setting. The series will begin with Aslam Chicken, known for its signature Butter Chicken, alongside Tandoori Chicken and Chicken Biryani, with other celebrated eateries joining the rotation over time.
“Old Delhi’s food culture is shaped by generations of culinary traditions and neighbourhood eateries that have become institutions in their own right. Through Legends of Delhi, we have an opportunity to bring these familiar flavours to a new audience while celebrating the people and stories behind them. Starting with Aslam Chicken, we look forward to showcasing more of the city's culinary heritage at Time Out Market Delhi,” says Anubhav Sapra, Founder, Delhi Food Walks.
So Tammy’s
Founded by Chef Tanmayi Arora and Prabhu Mundhra, So Tammy’s is a chef-led Mexican restaurant from Gurugram, known for its handcrafted tacos and bold flavours.
Their menu will feature favourites such as OG Lamb Birria, Baja Fish and Chipotle Jackfruit Piña tacos, alongside El Jefe Loaded Nachos and new dishes created exclusively for the Market, including the Charred Broccoli Taco and Pork Al Pastor.
“Delhi really loves its food. People here know what they like, but they’re always curious to try something new, and that keeps us experimenting. Time Out Market has a special place in our story. Years ago, Prabhu and I visited Time Out Market Lisboa and never forgot the experience. Opening at India’s first Time Out Market feels like life coming full circle. We’re excited to bring our much-loved handcrafted tacos, and a few new dishes created exclusively for the Market,” says Chef Tanmayi Arora, Co-founder, So Tammy’s.
These three join the previously announced kitchens, which include regional Indian street food with Bhawan, a burger and grill concept with Chard, and Japanese dining with Mizu Izakaya. Beyond its culinary offerings, Time Out Market Delhi will also host a variety of events, cultural experiences and engaging activations, bringing together food, entertainment and the city’s creative community. Further additions to the culinary line-up, details of the beverage programme and a first look at the Market’s events and cultural calendar will be announced in the lead-up to its opening in December 2026.
Time Out Studio will be the home of the Market’s programming and events, with cultural formats spanning art, theatre, music and comedy. It will also offer a space for private and corporate events, with the Market’s kitchens and bars available to cater to gatherings.
About Time Out Market Delhi
Time Out Market Delhi is a food and cultural destination at 5 Worldmark, Aerocity, New Delhi, opening in December 2026. Across approximately 25,000 sq. ft., it will have 11 kitchens, two full-service bars, a private events space, Time Out Studio, a live performance stage and seating for around 500 guests. It is brought to India by Quint Digital Limited (QDL), a digital and media-tech company focused on AI, which is the master franchise partner for Time Out Market and Time Out Media in India.
Time Out Market brings a city together under one roof: chefs, restaurateurs, drinks and cultural experiences, from live music to installations by local artists. The first opened in Lisbon in 2014, and there are now 13 Markets in cities including New York, Montréal, Dubai, Cape Town and Osaka. It is part of Time Out Group PLC (AIM: TMO), a global brand that connects people with city life through Time Out Media and Time Out Market. Time Out launched in London in 1968, and local experts now create and curate content on what to do, see and eat across more than 350 cities in over 50 countries.
For more information, please visit our website at https://www.timeout.com/time-out-market-delhi, and for the latest company news, visit our Press Office. In addition, connect with us on Instagram at @timeoutmarketdelhi.

title: 'There Will be Agitation': BJP's UCC Push in Bengal Hinges on Wooing Rajbongshis
description: West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari has vowed that the state will soon introduce laws against “love jihad” and “land jihad” under the UCC. But Rajbongshis in North Bengal are demanding exemption from the UCC. Will Suvendu Adhikari concur?
author: Rakhi Bose
content:
Six months into Suvendu Adhikari's tenure, West Bengal is witnessing shifts across its political, social, and cultural landscape. Follow The Quint's Bengal's Saffron Turn for in-depth coverage of these shifts. Become a member to power our ground reports.
"The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has betrayed the very people who voted for them. It did not fulfill any promises made to the people of North Bengal. Instead, it may now impose the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) on the Koch-Rajbongshi community and rob it of its indigenous identity," Bikash Roy Barman, activist and teacher from West Bengal's Cooch Behar, tells The Quint.
An Indigenous community, the Koch-Rajbongshis are governed by their distinct laws, customs, and cultural traditions. In the past few years, the community has voted for the BJP in large numbers—and is key to the party holding power across the hilly terrains in Cooch Behar and Jalpaiguri regions of North Bengal.
With West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari vowing that the state will soon introduce laws against “love jihad” and “land jihad” under the UCC—modelled on the laws in Uttarakhand and Gujarat—many within the Koch-Rajbongshis are alarmed.
