title: Home Ministry Warns WhatsApp Users Against Staying Logged In on Office Computers
description: The Union Home Ministry has warned WhatsApp users against leaving their accounts logged in on public or shared computers, as cybercriminals could misuse them to access private chats and carry out fraud. |National | Top Stories|
author: DY365
content:
Home Ministry Warns WhatsApp Users Against Staying Logged In on Office Computers
The Union Home Ministry has warned WhatsApp users against leaving their accounts logged in on public or shared computers, as cybercriminals could misuse them to access private chats and carry out fraud.
New Delhi: The Union Home Ministry has warned WhatsApp users not to leave their accounts logged in on computers, especially on shared or public devices. It said cybercriminals could use these open sessions to read private messages and misuse accounts to cheat others.
In its latest advisory, the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit of the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) said that an open WhatsApp Web account could allow strangers to read personal chats, see contact details and access group conversations. They could also send messages pretending to be the account owner and trick their friends and family members.
The agency has reminded users that simply closing the browser or WhatsApp Web tab does not log them out. Users must manually log out after every session to keep their accounts safe.
The advisory asks people to be careful while using WhatsApp Web on office computers, public computers or shared devices. It also advises users not to log in from cyber cafes, hotels and other public places. If using another computer is necessary, users should open WhatsApp Web in private or incognito mode.
The agency has also advised users not to share personal, financial or official information through WhatsApp Web on computers.
Users should regularly check their accounts for unusual activity, such as messages they did not send or strange replies from their contacts. These could be signs that someone else has accessed their account.
The I4C has also asked users to keep their computers, browsers and security software updated. It has warned against downloading unknown files or using cracked software.
The agency has urged everyone to follow these safety steps to protect their WhatsApp accounts and avoid online scams and financial fraud.

title: Bisleri Denies Reports of Unsafe Drinking Water, Says Samples Were Within Permissible Limits
description: After reports emerged claiming that Bisleri water was unsafe for consumption, the company issued a clarification, rejecting the claims that its packaged drinking water failed FSSAI safety tests. |National | Top Stories|
author: DY365
content:
Bisleri Denies Reports of Unsafe Drinking Water, Says Samples Were Within Permissible Limits
After reports emerged claiming that Bisleri water was unsafe for consumption, the company issued a clarification, rejecting the claims that its packaged drinking water failed FSSAI safety tests.
New Delhi: Bisleri has dismissed media reports claiming that its packaged drinking water was found unfit for consumption in tests conducted by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI).
In a clarification posted on X, the company said its water is safe for consumption and explained that the matter relates to a specific batch produced at its manufacturing unit in Goa in September 2025.
According to Bisleri, the FSSAI had collected six samples from the facility, of which five were found to be within the prescribed safety limits. However, the sixth sample recorded a bromate level of 12 micrograms per litre, slightly above the permissible limit of 10 micrograms per litre.
https://t.co/qOBmfxcYj9
— BisleriZone (@BisleriZone) November 23, 2026
Following this, Bisleri filed an appeal on November 22, 2025, and sent the sample to a referral laboratory for retesting. The laboratory found the bromate level to be within the prescribed limit but separately flagged the presence of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in the sample.
Due to the difference in the test results, Bisleri arranged for the same sample to be tested at another FSSAI-approved laboratory. The test again found the bromate level to be within the permissible limit.
The company said it submitted the test report to the FSSAI's Western Regional Office along with a formal letter on February 2, 2026. However, it claimed that it received no further communication from the authority and considered the matter closed.
Bisleri also stated that the alleged notice could not be found on the FSSAI's official website. It maintained that no such notice had been issued declaring its drinking water unsafe for consumption.
The company has reiterated that its packaged drinking water is safe, rejecting the claims circulating in media reports.

title: India, China Discuss Border Management and LAC Issues in Eastern Sector Talks
description: India and China recently held a meeting of their senior-most military commanders in the eastern sector, where the discussions focused on improving border management and addressing outstanding issues along LAC
author: Sentinel Digital Desk
content:
NEW DELHI: India and China recently held a meeting of their senior-most military commanders in the eastern sector, where the discussions focused on improving border management and addressing outstanding issues along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Wednesday. Addressing the weekly media briefing in New Delhi, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that India and China engage regularly through diplomatic and military mechanisms.
“India and China engage regularly through diplomatic and military mechanisms. A meeting of the senior-most military commanders was held in the eastern sector recently; discussion between the two sides focused on improving border management and addressing outstanding issues along the LAC. (IANS)

title: Massive Manhunt Underway for 65 Pakistani Terrorists in J-K Linked to LeT, JeM
description: Days after the killing of lone active local terrorist Lateef Bhat from Jammu and Kashmir soil, a massive hunt is on for 65 estimated Pakistani terrorists operating in the erstwhile state, having allegiance to banned terror outfits Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT), Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) and others
author: Sentinel Digital Desk
content:
NEW DELHI: Days after the killing of lone active local terrorist Lateef Bhat from Jammu and Kashmir soil, a massive hunt is on for 65 estimated Pakistani terrorists operating in the erstwhile state, having allegiance to banned terror outfits Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT), Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) and others, sources in the security establishment said.
Officials in the security establishment told ANI that these 65 Pakistani terrorists have been on the radar since their presence was confirmed by different intelligence wings within the system and it is learnt that the majority of them belong to the LeT and the JeM. Of the 65 foreign terrorists, 35 are linked to the LeT and 25 to the JeM, while the rest are from different outlawed terror outfits. (ANI)

title: S. Jaishankar, Russian FM exchanged views on bilateral, global issues: MEA
description: External Affairs Minister (EAM) S. Jaishankar and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov exchanged views on bilateral issues as well as multilateral and regional issues and ongoing conflicts during their recent telephone conversation
author: Sentinel Digital Desk
content:
NEW DELHI: External Affairs Minister (EAM) S. Jaishankar and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov exchanged views on bilateral issues as well as multilateral and regional issues and ongoing conflicts during their recent telephone conversation, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Wednesday.
Addressing the weekly media briefing in New Delhi, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that India has had several engagements with the Russian side in the last few weeks.
“Our Foreign Minister had a conversation with the Foreign Minister of Russia. We have had engagements with the Russian side — several such engagements in the last few weeks or so. And these are occasions when leaders from both sides, the External Affairs Minister from our side and the Foreign Minister of Russia from their side, exchange views on bilateral issues as well as several issues that today form part of the global landscape: multilateral issues, regional issues, conflicts that are going on. So these were some of the issues that were discussed during the phone call,” Jaiswal said. (IANS)

title: 2026 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay NIF Book Prize: Sam Dalrymple wins for debut book ‘Shattered Lands’
description: He will receive a cash prize of Rs 15 lakh on December 12 at the Bangalore Literature Festival.
author: Scroll Staff
content:
Sam Dalrymple’s debut book Shattered Lands: Five Partitions and the Making of Modern Asia is the winner of the 2026 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay NIF Book Prize 2026. He will be presented with the award, which will include a cash prize of Rs 15 lakh along with a trophy and a citation, at the Bangalore Literature Festival on December 12.
The Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay NIF Book Prize honours exceptional nonfiction writing on modern India. Shattered Lands was recognised for its account of the lesser-known partitions of British India. Where most accounts of Partition begin and end in 1947, Dalrymple follows the empire’s dissolution across five fractures, from Burma to Aden.
This year’s jury comprised Chairman of Tata Sons and Tata Group N Chandrasekaran, political scientist and chair of KCBP NIF Jury Niraja Gopal Jayal, partner at Trilegal Rahul Matthan, historian of science Jahnavi Phalkey, historian Srinath Raghavan, former Foreign Secretary of India Nirupama Rao, and entrepreneur Manish Sabharwal.
The jury citation noted that Shattered Lands is an “illuminating exploration of the historical and political forces that shaped the Indian subcontinent. With remarkable depth of research and compelling storytelling, Sam Dalrymple brings to life the intertwined histories of a region divided by borders, yet bound by shared pasts. An ambitious and compelling work of history, the book offers fresh perspectives on Partition and its enduring legacies. ”

title: How Telugu translations of Shakespeare’s plays changed culture in 19th-century Madras Presidency
description: An excerpt from ‘Travelling Texts: Translating Nineteenth-Century European Classics into Indian Languages’, edited by Shantanu Majee and K Subramanyam.
author: Nishi Pulugurtha
content:
The map of bhashas
The term “bhasha” signifies “language” in many South Asian tongues, but it also evokes the rootedness of vernacular identity – the earth-bound tongues spoken not in courtly, colonial, or cosmopolitan registers but in practices of everyday life. Across India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Nepal, bhasha literatures are rich in history, folklore, philosophy and resistance.
Yet historically, these literatures have often been overshadowed – first by the dominance of colonial presence, and later, by the prominence of a few “major” languages like Hindi, Bengali or Tamil.
The process of translating European classics into South Asian bhashas raises complex ethical questions. To what extent can a translator adapt a source text without distorting its intent? Is fidelity owed to the original’s linguistic structure or to its philosophical substance? This act of cultural transcreation becomes even more charged in postcolonial contexts. Translation is not merely literary; it becomes political. The prestige of European classics, often valorised through colonial education systems, means their entry into bhasha literatures is often both aspirational and subversive.
By translating Dostoevsky into Bengali, then, a bhasha translator both affirms the universality of the Russian’s themes and asserts the vernacular’s capacity to absorb and reinterpret the global canon.
Travelling with words
Unlike translation between major world languages (say, French and English), translation between South Asian bhashas often involves multiple modes of mediation. Sometimes a work moves first into Hindi, then into English, then into Marathi, picking up layers and distortions like a snowball. Each translation is a fresh departure and arrival: no two voyages are the same.
Take, for instance, the epic Silappadikaram of Tamil, one of the foundational texts of ancient Indian literature. When rendered into Malayalam, Telugu or Kannada, the work doesn’t simply cross into different scripts; it reorients itself towards new mythologies of place and body. The anklet that causes devastation in Madurai may, in another language’s retelling, seem to chime slightly differently, evoking local memories of betrayal, fidelity and injustice.
Scholars like GN Devy and AK Ramanujan have emphasised that bhasha literatures are intensely tied to their regional soil – their idioms saturated with climate, cuisine, caste and cosmology. An old proverb confirms that if at every three or four kilometres the water tastes different in this country, then there’s a different tongue to be heard at every 12–15. Therefore, every translation embodies a travel itself – not merely moving the text but “replanting” it in new soil, where it must adapt, sometimes thriving, sometimes transforming beyond recognition.
Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak also refers to the “intimate act” of translation – one that recognises both the alterity of the source text and the demands of the receiving culture. In this context, translation is not a bridge between static points. It is a caravanserai, a moving camp of meanings.
The dangers of travel
Yet, travel is not innocent. Travellers bring with them baggage; translators bring their own histories, politics and unconscious biases. In South Asia, where language often intersects with religion, caste and class, translation can become a deeply political act. When the Tirukkural, a seminal Tamil ethical text, was translated into Sanskrit and later Hindi, there were accusations of “Sanskritisation” – of imposing Brahminical values onto a text celebrated for its secular and egalitarian spirit. Similarly, Dalit literature, when translated from Marathi or Kannada into English or Hindi, often undergoes a softening of its rawness, a domestication of its rage to make it palatable to upper-caste or global readers.
– an excerpt from the Preface by Shantanu Majee.
Colonial education in India resulted in several English literary texts being taught and read in 19th-century India. Among them were plays by Shakespeare. The history of Shakespeare in India can be traced back to the colonial encounter, to the study, performances, recitations, and translations of Shakespeare into several Indian languages. The National Library in Kolkata recorded several Shakespeare translations and adaptations done in the various Indian languages till the year 1964.
Of a total of 670 such records, 128 were in Bengali, 97 in Marathi, 83 in Tamil, 70 in Hindi, 66 in Kannada and 62 in Telugu. The latter half of the 19th century was witness to a literary revival in Telugu that was strongly marked by the influence of Sanskrit and English literature. There were also translations of works from these two languages during the period.
The translations and adaptations of Shakespeare’s plays into Telugu created a corpus of literary texts, both in prose and dramatic forms, that reveal that the plays of Shakespeare were no longer just texts to be studied but were becoming an important part of the cultural scenario as well.
Telugu was a language spoken in the Madras Presidency in the nineteenth century. Madras Presidency or Madras Province, was an administrative province of British India. It was officially referred to as the Presidency of Fort St George. This province included the states of present-day Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, some areas of modern-day Kerala, Karnataka, Odisha and Telangana as well.
The city of Madras (present-day Chennai) was the winter capital while the hill station of Ooty was the summer capital. The languages spoken here were Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada, Odia and Tulu. Telugu was the language spoken in the districts to the north of the city of Madras and to the east of Bellary (now part of Karnataka) and Anantapur (in present-day Andhra Pradesh) districts. The 1871 census noted a total of 11,610,000 people who spoke Telugu in the Madras Presidency which increased in the 1901 census to 14,276,509.
During the times of India’s independence in 1947, Tamil and Telugu speakers comprised over 78% of the total population of the Madras Presidency. Today Telugu is the language spoken in two states – Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
Theatrical performances in Telugu chiefly consisted of Kuchipudi performances, dance dramas based on the puranas and folk forms like the burrakatha (an oral form of storytelling that includes songs, prayers, dialogues and music) and the tholibomma aata (literally the art of leather puppets, a performance with shadow puppets).
In the latter part of the 19th century, a change was noticed. This was due to the Parsi theatre companies from Bombay touring various parts of the Madras Presidency. These performances led to local people forming drama companies and resulted in productions and performances in the Telugu language. The influence of Parsi theatre groups that toured various parts of the south of India in the nineteenth century had a great influence on the way Shakespeare found its way into the cultural and literary ethos of the Telugu people.
The Dharwar School from Maharashtra was another popular group that influenced Telugu theatre. These touring groups were an important form of entertainment in South India. Their success and popularity led to the formation of local language drama groups that often staged plays based on the works of Kalidasa and Shakespeare. These performances led to the development of Telugu theatre companies, chief among them being Surabhi Theatre.
Plays performed were chiefly based on stories from Indian mythology and the epics. Sanskrit plays were being translated for performance in Telugu as well. One such play was Sakuntala, a play in which actors rendered the Sanskrit shlokas followed by the Telugu translation of them. This was the translation done by Kandukuri Veerasalingam.
An important name in Telugu translations from Sanskrit is Vedam Venkataraya Sastry (1853–1929), a poet, dramatist and critic, who wrote plays in Telugu and translated Sanskrit plays by Kalidasa and Harsha. His translations of Kalidasa’s Vikramorvasiya (1901) and Harsha’s Nagananda (1891) were well-known and popular. Two of his Telugu plays are Prataparudriya natakam (1897) and Usha natakam (1901). The word natakam means a play.
In 1876, Vavilala Vasudeva Sastri (1851–1897) translated Julius Caesar. A pioneer in translating Shakespeare into Telugu, his translation retained the names of the characters of the source text while adapting them to the Telugu language. Julius Caesar becomes “Juliusudu”, Brutus becomes “Brutusudu” in the translation. Sastri uses the common suffix used in Telugu while referring to the names of people here. The translation was done in verse, in a metre that the translator believed was closest to the iambic pentametre.
In 1880, Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice was translated as Venusu Vanija Naatakamu. Gurazada Sriramamurti (1851–1899), who translated the play, used both prose and verse in the translation. He also used the names of the dramatis personae as they appeared in the source text. Gurazada Sriramamurti was a scholar in the court of King Ananda Gajapathiraju of Vizianagaram and is known as the first person who wrote the biography in Telugu – Kavijivitamu (Lives of Poets, 1893). CSR Krishnamma translated Macbeth – a Telugu prose translation that was done in 1895. Lady Macbeth and Lady Macduff become Macbeth Devi and Macduff Devi in the translation.
In 1880, Kandukuri Veeresalingam (1848–1919) began an association for Telugu drama in the Madras Presidency. He wrote a play in Telugu – Vyavahara Dharma Bodhini. He also translated William Shakespeare’s Comedy of Errors into Telugu, his mother tongue, as Chamatkara Ratnavali. The drama association that he began staged both these plays in Telugu on April 16, 1880; the performers were his students.
In the same year, he translated Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice from Tales from Shakespeare by Charles and Mary Lamb. Printed at Vivekavarthani Press in Rajahmundry in the year 1880, the translation had on its front cover this description of the author/translator as “Kandukuri Veerasalingam, Telugu Pundit, First Grade Government College, Rajahmundry.”
Kandukuri Veeresalingam, often referred to as the father of modern Telugu literature, translated Charles and Mary Lamb’s Tales from Shakespeare in a very simple style. The names of characters were changed. Situations and incidents that would fit the Telugu ethos were used in the translation. In 1880, Kandukuri notes in his autobiography that he had begun a translation of The Merchant of Venice with the title Venusu Vartakuni Charitramu.
Kandukuri Veeresalingam was not just a writer and translator. Often referred to as Veerasalingam Pantalu, he was an important social reformer of the time and was a strong advocate of women’s education, widow remarriage and the abolition of child marriage. Kandukuri Veerasalingam’s life and work reveal the amalgamation of the political, social and cultural environment of the times.
Missionary activity in the region had resulted in the building of several churches in the area, and English education was seen in Andhra as well. In 1840, Lord Hay began the first Anglo-vernacular school in the region. Soon, several other such schools were set up in the region.
Samuel Dey, an American Baptist missionary, founded the Telugu Baptist Church in 1840 in Nellore. Till 1805, it was the Roman Catholic missionaries who worked in this region (which, after 1950, was formed into the state of Andhra Pradesh). After 1805, the Protestants began to propagate Christianity in the region as well. Visakhapatnam became an important centre for religion, and the Bible and other books were translated into Telugu. Like the Scottish missionaries who set up educational institutions in Calcutta, the Noble College was set up by missionaries who came to Machilipatnam in 1841.
The Charter Act of 1813 led to the free entry of missionaries into India, though it took some years for the spread of missionary activity. Sir Arthur Cotton, a military engineer who toured the Godavari delta region in 1833, worked to create a mission station in the region. Cotton supervised the construction of the Godavari Barrage near Dhavaleswaram and the rail bridge across the Godavari River connecting Rajahmundry and Kovvur.
On his way back from England in 1836, Cotton brought with him several missionaries, two of whom set up what later came to be called the Godavari Delta Mission that had its headquarters at Narsapur. Besides its evangelical work, the Godavari Delta Mission set up schools in the region and the Mission Hospital at Narsapur. It was missionary activity that led to the setting up of the first Anglo-Telugu school in 1844, which was the first Anglo-vernacular school in Andhra Pradesh.
In 1853, Mrs Hay began a school where the girls were given education as well as training to become teachers. The missionaries also had a printing press at Visakhapatnam that printed religious books in the Telugu language. It is these activities that led to an interest in English education and, with it, social reform as well. The nineteenth century was a time of social reform in various parts of India, and the Telugu-speaking people were part of this intellectual and social ferment as well.
Like many other reformers of the time, Kandukuri Veerasalingam strongly believed in Western science and advancement and considered English education important in order to rejuvenate Telugu culture and literature. In 1875, he wrote:
It is admitted by one and all that western lore has worked wonders among the natives of India. We are quite aware that English education has rendered natives more refined in their manners, has dispelled the mist of superstition from the minds of several of them, if not many, and has considerably developed their moral calibre whenever it is properly imparted.
It was, therefore, imperative to find ways to make this “western lore” available to those who did not have access to English education. Kandukuri believed that translation into Telugu would be a way to make English texts available to Telugu people. Kandukuri Veerasalingam is also credited with the modernisation of the language of Telugu literature, in that the language of literature moved from the classical style to the use of a more colloquial form. This also meant an increase in the use of prose in the genres of the essay, biography, autobiography and the novel in Telugu.
Excerpted with permission from ‘Shakespeare in Telugu in the Nineteenth Century’ by Nishi Pulugurtha in Travelling Texts: Translating Nineteenth-Century European Classics into Indian Languages, edited by Shantanu Majee and K Subramanyam, Routledge.

title: A new book recounts how one honest conversation helped Ford survive the 2008 financial crisis
description: An excerpt from ‘Nobody Wins Alone: The Magic of Teamwork’, by Prakash Iyer.
author: Prakash Iyer
content:
In 2006, the Ford Motor Company was in deep trouble. The company was losing billions of dollars. Market share was sliding. The factories were bloated. And Detroit had begun to whisper that the mighty, iconic automotive giant might not survive.
A new chief executive walked into that crisis. His name was Alan Mulally. A man who had spent his whole career at Boeing, building aeroplanes. The car industry veterans smirked. What would a plane guy know about cars?
Mulally started a simple ritual at Ford. Every Thursday morning, his top leaders gathered for what he called the “business plan review”. Each of them presented updates on their part of the business, using colour codes. Green meant on track. Yellow meant caution. Red meant trouble.
At the first meeting, as he sat through the business presentations, he saw something remarkable. Slide after slide after slide was green. Every division, every region, every function. An unbroken sea of green.
He stopped the meeting. And asked a question that began Ford’s turnaround. “We are going to lose billions of dollars this year,” he said. “Isn’t there something that is not going well here? How come I am only seeing green?” he wondered aloud.
Nobody moved. Nobody spoke. Because everyone in that room had grown up in a culture where a red slide meant a career problem. Admitting there was trouble was seen as a sign of weakness. The messenger got shot long before the message was heard. And the company struggled even while all the slides glowed green.
A few weeks later, one man decided to test whether the new boss meant it.
Mark Fields was the man in charge of Ford’s business in the Americas. He was facing a real problem. A faulty part threatened to delay the launch of the Ford Edge, one of the company’s most important new vehicles. He could have painted it green and prayed, the way everyone always had, all along. Instead, at that Thursday meeting, he put up his slide. Red. Shocking, bright, hard-to-miss red.
The room went quiet. People stared at the table. By some accounts, colleagues shifted their chairs away from him. Picture that. The corporate version of stepping back from a man about to be struck by lightning. Mark had already told his family he might be fired that week.
And then Alan Mulally began to clap.
“That is great visibility, Mark,” he said. He then turned to the room and asked who could help Mark with the problem. Within seconds, a quality expert offered his team. Another division head said his business had seen the same fault before and quickly shared the fix. The launch was saved. And Mark Fields didn’t just keep his job. Some years later, he succeeded Mulally as chief executive of Ford.
But the real change came the following Thursday. As the businesses presented their updates, the screen began to look like a rainbow. Red, yellow and green everywhere. The truth had come out of hiding. Mulally later said that was the exact moment he knew Ford would make it. Because his leadership team was finally working on reality rather than on beautifully formatted fiction. Ford went on to survive the 2008 financial crisis as the only major American carmaker that did not need a government bailout.
A boss of mine once gave me a phrase for what Mulally saw in that first meeting. The watermelon dashboard. “Watch out for them,” he told me. They are green on the outside. But cut it open, and it is red all the way through.
Every organisation has a few of these watermelon dashboard moments. The project that reports green every fortnight, right up to the week it slips by six months. The account that is doing great, great, great and then gone. The team that is high on engagement until three people resign in a month. Nobody lied really. They simply understood what colour was welcome in the room.
So, what are you clapping for in your meetings? Remember your team is watching what you applaud. Applaud only the good news and good news is all you will get. No matter what is actually happening. Punish the red slide, even gently, with a frown or a sharp question or a little coldness afterwards and you have taught everyone what to do. Problems do not disappear when you make them unwelcome. They go underground. They grow in the dark. And they surface later as full-blown disasters.
And if you are the one holding the red slide, wondering if you should present it, take heart from Mark Fields. The room may go quiet. People might move their chairs away. But you might just save the launch. And you might even find yourself in the corner office someday.
So here is a question for you. When did somebody last bring you genuinely bad news? Not just a small hiccup. But a real problem, brought to you early, while it could still be fixed.
If you cannot remember, you should be worried. Because it does not mean your team has no problems. It means you are looking at a watermelon.
The first job of a leader is to make it safe for people to tell the truth. To tell the whole story, as it is. Like Alan Mulally did. The clapping is optional. But it helps.
Excerpted with permission from Nobody Wins Alone: The Magic of Teamwork, Prakash Iyer, Penguin India.

title: संविधान दिवस विशेष: संविधान के वे ख़ास प्रावधान जो हाशिये के समाज को बराबरी का हक़ देते हैं
description: संविधान दिवस (26 नवंबर) पर जानें आरक्षण से आगे संविधान के वे विशेष प्रावधान (भाग-16, अनुच्छेद 46, 244, 338 और पांचवीं-छठवीं अनुसूची), जो दलितों, आदिवासियों और वंचित वर्गों को बराबरी और सम्मान का हक़ देते हैं।
author: Rajan Chaudhary
content:
हमारे देश में जब भी संविधान और वंचित समाज.... दलितों, आदिवासियों, पिछड़ों और महिलाओं के अधिकारों की बात चलती है, तो पूरी बहस अक्सर एक ही शब्द पर आकर अटक जाती है... आरक्षण। चाय की दुकानों से लेकर टीवी के स्टूडियो तक, लोग सरकारी नौकरियों और कॉलेजों की सीटों के गणित में ही उलझे रहते हैं।
लेकिन क्या भारतीय संविधान ने हाशिये पर धकेल दिए गए करोड़ों लोगों के लिए सिर्फ़ कुछ सीटें ही तय की थीं?
बिल्कुल नहीं। 26 नवंबर 1949 को जब संविधान सभा ने इस ऐतिहासिक दस्तावेज़ को अपनाया, तो उसके निर्माताओं के सामने एक सीधा और कठिन सवाल था.... एक ऐसे समाज में जहाँ सदियों तक जन्म के आधार पर इंसान की हैसियत, उसकी ज़मीन, उसकी शिक्षा और यहाँ तक कि उसके चलने का रास्ता तक तय होता रहा हो, वहाँ सबको एक ही लाइन में बराबरी पर कैसे खड़ा किया जाए?
इसका जवाब सिर्फ़ आरक्षण नहीं था। संविधान ने एक ऐसा मज़बूत ढाँचा खड़ा किया, जो वंचित समाज को सत्ता में हिस्सेदारी, जल-जंगल-ज़मीन पर अधिकार, आर्थिक सुरक्षा और अन्याय के ख़िलाफ़ लड़ने के लिए स्वतंत्र संस्थाएँ देता है। आज संविधान दिवस पर, आइए आरक्षण की शोरगुल भरी बहस से थोड़ा आगे बढ़कर संविधान के उन विशेष प्रावधानों को जानते हैं, जो हाशिये के समाज को सचमुच बराबरी का हक़ देते हैं।
लोकतंत्र में बदलाव तब नहीं आता जब कोई और आपके लिए दया दिखाकर फ़ैसले ले; बदलाव तब आता है जब आप ख़ुद उस मेज़ पर बैठते हैं जहाँ कानून बनते हैं। संविधान के भाग-16 में अनुच्छेद 330 (लोकसभा) और अनुच्छेद 332 (राज्यों की विधानसभाओं) के ज़रिए अनुसूचित जातियों और अनुसूचित जनजातियों के लिए राजनीतिक प्रतिनिधित्व सुनिश्चित किया गया है।
बात सिर्फ़ संसद और विधानसभा तक नहीं रुकी। बाद में संविधान के भाग-9 (अनुच्छेद 243घ) और भाग-9-क (अनुच्छेद 243न) के माध्यम से पंचायतों और नगरपालिकाओं में भी वंचित वर्गों और महिलाओं की भागीदारी तय की गई। इसका असर आज गाँव की चौपाल से लेकर देश की संसद तक दिखता है... जिन समुदायों को कभी गाँव के फैसलों में बोलने तक की इजाज़त नहीं थी, वे आज सरपंच, विधायक और सांसद बनकर नीतियां तय कर रहे हैं।
आदिवासी समाज के लिए जंगल सिर्फ़ पेड़-पौधों का इलाका नहीं है, वह उनकी संस्कृति, आजीविका और पहचान है। संविधान निर्माता इस संवेदनशीलता को गहराई से समझते थे। इसलिए उन्होंने भाग-10 (अनुच्छेद 244 और 244क) के साथ-साथ पांचवीं और छठवीं अनुसूची के रूप में एक अभेद्य सुरक्षा कवच बनाया।
पांचवीं अनुसूची देश के विभिन्न राज्यों में अनुसूचित क्षेत्रों के प्रशासन और जनजातियों के हितों की रक्षा करती है, ताकि बाहरी दखल से उनकी ज़मीन और संसाधन न छिने जाएँ। वहीं, छठवीं अनुसूची पूर्वोत्तर के राज्यों (असम, मेघालय, त्रिपुरा और मिज़ोरम) के जनजातीय क्षेत्रों को स्वशासी परिषदों के ज़रिए अपने नियम और परंपराएँ बचाने का अधिकार देती है। यह प्रावधान इस बात की गारंटी है कि विकास के नाम पर किसी समाज की जड़ें नहीं उखाड़ी जा सकतीं।
अधिकार कागज़ पर लिख देना आसान है, लेकिन जब कोई ताक़तवर व्यवस्था उन्हें कुचलने की कोशिश करे, तो वंचित इंसान किसका दरवाज़ा खटखटाए? इसी चिंता का हल संविधान ने स्वतंत्र आयोगों के रूप में निकाला। अनुच्छेद 338 के तहत राष्ट्रीय अनुसूचित जाति आयोग और अनुच्छेद 338क के तहत राष्ट्रीय अनुसूचित जनजाति आयोग का गठन किया गया। इसी तरह, अनुच्छेद 340 पिछड़े वर्गों की सामाजिक और शैक्षणिक दशाओं की जाँच के लिए आयोग बनाने का रास्ता खोलता है।
ये आयोग महज़ सरकारी दफ़्तर नहीं हैं। इनके पास किसी भी उत्पीड़न, भेदभाव या अधिकारों के हनन की जाँच करने, अधिकारियों को तलब करने और सरकार को जवाबदेह ठहराने की संवैधानिक ताक़त होती है। इसके अलावा अनुच्छेद 339 केंद्र सरकार को यह ज़िम्मेदारी देता है कि वह राज्यों में अनुसूचित जनजातियों के कल्याण और उनके क्षेत्रों के प्रशासन की निगरानी करे।
हाशिये के समाज की सबसे बड़ी पीड़ा सिर्फ़ ग़रीबी नहीं थी, बल्कि वह व्यवस्था थी जिसने उनसे बिना मज़दूरी के काम (बेगारी) करवाया और उन्हें अछूत मानकर इंसान के दर्जे से नीचे रखा। संविधान के अनुच्छेद 17 ने अस्पृश्यता (छुआछूत) को जड़ से खत्म करते हुए इसे अपराध घोषित किया।
इसी के साथ अनुच्छेद 23 (मानव के दुर्व्यापार और बलात्श्रम का प्रतिषेध) ने सदियों से चली आ रही बंधुआ मज़दूरी और बेगारी पर ताला लगा दिया। आज कोई भी व्यक्ति किसी मज़दूर से ज़बरदस्ती या बिना वाजिब मज़दूरी के काम नहीं ले सकता। यह प्रावधान उस हर इंसान के स्वाभिमान की रक्षा करता है, जिसकी मेहनत को पीढ़ियों तक मुफ़्त का हक़ समझा जाता रहा।
संविधान केवल भेदभाव रोकने तक सीमित नहीं है, वह सरकारों को आगे बढ़कर मदद करने का निर्देश भी देता है। राज्य की नीति के निदेशक तत्वों (भाग-4) में शामिल अनुच्छेद 46 सरकार को स्पष्ट आदेश देता है कि वह अनुसूचित जातियों, अनुसूचित जनजातियों और समाज के अन्य दुर्बल वर्गों के शिक्षा और आर्थिक हितों को विशेष सावधानी से बढ़ाए, और सामाजिक अन्याय व हर तरह के शोषण से उनकी रक्षा करे।
वहीं, अनुच्छेद 39क (समान न्याय और निःशुल्क विधिक सहायता) यह सुनिश्चित करता है कि किसी ग़रीब या वंचित व्यक्ति को सिर्फ़ इसलिए न्याय से वंचित न होना पड़े क्योंकि उसके पास वकील करने के पैसे नहीं हैं।
संविधान दिवस पर इन प्रावधानों को याद करना इसलिए ज़रूरी है, क्योंकि अक्सर इन्हें किसी 'रियायत' या 'खैरात' की तरह पेश किया जाता है। सच यह है कि ये प्रावधान किसी पर एहसान नहीं हैं.... ये एक सदियों से अन्याय झेलते रहे समाज के साथ किया गया वह वादा हैं, जिसके बिना भारत एक सच्चा लोकतंत्र नहीं बन सकता।
डॉ. बी.आर. आंबेडकर ने कहा था कि राजनीतिक लोकतंत्र तब तक नहीं टिक सकता, जब तक उसकी नींव में सामाजिक लोकतंत्र न हो। आरक्षण तो उस इमारत की सिर्फ़ एक ईंट है; असली इमारत संविधान के इन्हीं विशेष प्रावधानों पर टिकी है, जो हर सुबह हाशिये के आखिरी व्यक्ति के कंधे पर हाथ रखकर कहती है—डरो मत, यह देश उतना ही तुम्हारा भी है।
द मूकनायक की प्रीमियम और चुनिंदा खबरें अब द मूकनायक के न्यूज़ एप्प पर पढ़ें। Google Play Store से न्यूज़ एप्प इंस्टाल करने के लिए यहां क्लिक करें.
'द मूकनायक' जनवादी पत्रकारिता करता है. यह संविधान, लोकतंत्र और सामाजिक न्याय पर चलने वाला मीडिया समूह है। अगर आप भी चाहते हैं कि 'द मूकनायक' हमेशा हाशिए पर खड़े लोगों की आवाज बुलंद करता रहे, बेजुबानों की पीड़ा दिखाते रहें तो सब्सक्राइब करें।

title: संविधान विशेष स्पेशल: वे 7 अनुच्छेद जो हर भारतीय को ताक़तवर बनाते हैं
description: 26 नवंबर को संविधान दिवस पर जानें भारतीय संविधान के वे 7 सबसे ताक़तवर अनुच्छेद (14, 15, 17, 19, 21, 25 और 32), जो किताबों से निकलकर हर आम भारतीय की ज़िंदगी और अधिकारों की रक्षा करते हैं।
author: Rajan Chaudhary
content:
सुबह-सुबह किसी कस्बे के नुक्कड़ पर चाय की चुस्की लेते हुए जब कोई आम आदमी सरकार की नीति पर बेझिझक बहस करता है, जब किसी गाँव की पहली पीढ़ी की बेटी बस्ता उठाकर कॉलेज के गेट से भीतर कदम रखती है, या जब कोई दिहाड़ी मज़दूर अपने पसीने की पूरी मज़दूरी के लिए ठेकेदार की आँखों में आँखें डालकर बात करता है—तो उस वक़्त वे शायद संविधान की कोई मोटी किताब लेकर नहीं चल रहे होते। लेकिन उनके पीछे एक अदृश्य कवच खड़ा होता है।
वह कवच 77 साल पहले आज ही के दिन, 26 नवंबर 1949 को गढ़ा गया था।
अक्सर हम संविधान को संसद की लाइब्रेरी में रखी कोई भारी-भरकम कानूनी किताब या प्रतियोगी परीक्षाओं के सिलेबस तक सीमित कर देते हैं। 26 नवंबर को संविधान दिवस पर कुछ संदेश फॉरवर्ड होते हैं, प्रस्तावना पढ़ी जाती है और शाम होते-होते सब सामान्य हो जाता है। लेकिन सच यह है कि संविधान किसी संग्रहालय में सजाकर रखने की चीज़ नहीं है, यह वह ताक़त है जो हर सुबह आपको बिना डरे, सिर उठाकर जीने का हौसला देती है।
आइए, आज संविधान दिवस पर किताबी भाषा को किनारे रखकर भारतीय संविधान के भाग-3 (मूल अधिकार) के उन 7 अनुच्छेदों को समझते हैं, जो कागज़ पर नहीं, बल्कि हमारी रोज़मर्रा की ज़िंदगी में धड़कते हैं।
जिस देश में सदियों तक न्याय इस बात से तय होता था कि अपराध करने वाला किस घराने या किस पायदान से आता है, वहाँ अनुच्छेद 14 (विधि के समक्ष समता) ने एक झटके में सारा खेल बदल दिया। यह अनुच्छेद कहता है कि कानून की तराजू पर एक बड़े उद्योगपति, एक नेता और एक रिक्शाचालक का वज़न एक बराबर है। कोई भी व्यक्ति, चाहे उसका पद कितना ही बड़ा क्यों न हो, कानून से ऊपर नहीं है। जब भी आप किसी ताक़तवर के खिलाफ़ थाने या अदालत में खड़े होने की हिम्मत जुटाते हैं, तो वह हिम्मत आपको अनुच्छेद 14 से मिलती है।
हमारे समाज में भेदभाव की जड़ें कितनी गहरी रही हैं, यह किसी से छिपा नहीं है। लेकिन अनुच्छेद 15 (धर्म, मूलवंश, जाति, लिंग या जन्म स्थान के आधार पर विभेद का प्रतिषेध) इस समाज को एक नई नैतिकता देता है। यह साफ़ करता है कि राज्य या कोई भी सार्वजनिक स्थान... चाहे वह स्कूल हो, अस्पताल हो, होटल हो, सड़क हो या गाँव का कुआँ... किसी के लिए सिर्फ़ इसलिए बंद नहीं हो सकता कि उसका धर्म, जाति, लिंग या जन्म स्थान अलग है। यह अनुच्छेद उस हर दीवार को गिराता है जो इंसान को इंसान से बाँटती है।
संविधान का यह एक ऐसा अनुच्छेद है, जिसे पढ़ते हुए आज भी रोंगटे खड़े हो जाते हैं। अनुच्छेद 17 (अस्पृश्यता का अंत) सिर्फ़ एक कानूनी धारा नहीं है, यह करोड़ों लोगों को सदियों के मौन अपमान से बाहर निकालने का ऐतिहासिक ऐलान है। संविधान निर्माताओं ने छुआछूत को केवल 'बुरी सामाजिक प्रथा' कहकर नहीं छोड़ा, बल्कि इसे एक दंडनीय अपराध घोषित किया। आज अगर कोई किसी की परछाई, पानी या मटके को लेकर अपमान करने की जुर्रत करे, तो कानून उसके सामने दीवार बनकर खड़ा हो जाता है।
लोकतंत्र सिर्फ़ पाँच साल में एक बार वोट डालने से ज़िंदा नहीं रहता, वह ज़िंदा रहता है नागरिकों की आवाज़ से। अनुच्छेद 19 (वाक्-स्वातंत्र्य आदि विषयक कुछ अधिकारों का संरक्षण) हर भारतीय को बोलने, लिखने, असहमति जताने और शांतिपूर्ण ढंग से इकट्ठा होने की आज़ादी देता है। इतना ही नहीं, यही अनुच्छेद आपको यह हक़ भी देता है कि आप देश के किसी भी कोने में जाकर बस सकें और अपनी पसंद का काम-धंधा या पेशा चुन सकें। आज अगर एक किसान का बेटा शहर जाकर पत्रकार, डॉक्टर या कारोबारी बन पाता है, तो उसके पंखों में हवा अनुच्छेद 19 ही भरता है।
शायद पूरे संविधान में सबसे जीवंत और लगातार विस्तृत होता अनुच्छेद यही है। अनुच्छेद 21 (प्राण और दैहिक स्वतंत्रता का संरक्षण) के शब्दों की गिनती कम है, लेकिन इसका दायरा आसमान जितना बड़ा है। अदालतों ने बार-बार यह साफ़ किया है कि 'जीवन के अधिकार' का मतलब सिर्फ़ पशुओं की तरह साँस लेते रहना नहीं है... इसका मतलब है गरिमा के साथ जीने का अधिकार। इसमें आपकी निजता (Privacy), साफ़ हवा-पानी, आजीविका, इलाज, यहाँ तक कि अपनी पसंद का जीवनसाथी चुनने और सम्मान के साथ जीने का हक़ भी शामिल है। यह अनुच्छेद सुनिश्चित करता है कि सत्ता मनमाने ढंग से किसी की आज़ादी या जान नहीं छीन सकती।
भारत की खूबसूरती इसकी विविधता में है... यहाँ सुबह की अज़ान, मंदिर की घंटी, गुरुद्वारे की अरदास और चर्च की प्रार्थना एक ही हवा में घुलती है। अनुच्छेद 25 (अंतःकरण की और धर्म को अबाध रूप से मानने, आचरण और प्रचार करने की स्वतंत्रता) इस विविधता की गारंटी है। यह हर नागरिक को यह भरोसा देता है कि वह किस ईश्वर को माने, कैसे प्रार्थना करे.... या किसी भी धर्म को न माने... यह पूरी तरह उसका निजी फ़ैसला है। आपकी आस्था पर किसी और का पहरा नहीं हो सकता।
कल्पना कीजिए कि आपके पास ऊपर लिखे सारे अधिकार कागज़ पर तो हैं, लेकिन अगर कोई सरकार, अधिकारी या ताक़तवर व्यक्ति उन्हें छीन ले, तो आप क्या करेंगे? यहीं आता है अनुच्छेद 32 (संवैधानिक उपचारों का अधिकार)। बाबा साहेब डॉ. बी.आर. आंबेडकर ने इसे 'संविधान का हृदय और आत्मा' कहा था। यह अनुच्छेद आम नागरिक के हाथ में वह सीधी चाबी देता है, जिससे वह अपने मूल अधिकारों के हनन पर सीधे देश के सर्वोच्च न्यायालय (सुप्रीम कोर्ट) का दरवाज़ा खटखटा सकता है। बिना अनुच्छेद 32 के बाकी सारे अधिकार सिर्फ़ अच्छी लगने वाली कविता बनकर रह जाते।
संविधान दिवस हमें सिर्फ़ अतीत पर गर्व करने के लिए नहीं बुलाता, वह हमें आईना भी दिखाता है। बाबा साहेब डॉ. आंबेडकर ने संविधान सभा के अपने अंतिम भाषण में चेतावनी दी थी कि कोई भी संविधान चाहे कितना ही अच्छा क्यों न हो, अगर उसे लागू करने वाले लोग बुरे हों, तो वह बुरा साबित हो सकता है। और संविधान को बचाने की ज़िम्मेदारी सिर्फ़ जजों या नेताओं की नहीं है, यह हम नागरिकों की है।
जिस दिन हर भारतीय इन 7 अनुच्छेदों को सिर्फ़ याद नहीं, बल्कि महसूस करने लगेगा, जिस दिन वह अपने हक़ के साथ-साथ अपने पड़ोसी के हक़ के लिए भी खड़ा होने लगेगा, उस दिन सच में संविधान कागज़ से उतरकर हमारी ज़िंदगी में पूरी तरह लागू हो जाएगा।
द मूकनायक की प्रीमियम और चुनिंदा खबरें अब द मूकनायक के न्यूज़ एप्प पर पढ़ें। Google Play Store से न्यूज़ एप्प इंस्टाल करने के लिए यहां क्लिक करें.

title: 121 kg gold, 45 ornaments: Tirumala Temple gets biggest-ever individual offering worth Rs 160 crore
description: The Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD) has received a massive offering of 121 kg of gold ornaments for Lord Venkateswara at the Tirumala temple. The donation, comprising 45 ornaments arranged in nine sets, is estimated to be worth between Rs 150 crore and Rs 160 crore, making it the largest individual offering ever made to the famous hill shrine, according to government and TTD sources.

title: SC quashes early release of former MP Anand Mohan in murder case, orders him to surrender within a month
description: The Supreme Court has set aside the premature release of former Bihar MP Anand Mohan in the 1994 murder case of the then Gopalganj District Magistrate G. Krishnaiah. The court has declared the Bihar government's 2023 amendment to its remission rules unconstitutional and directed Anand Mohan to surrender within a month to return to prison. Anand Mohan was convicted in the case involving the killing of IAS officer G. Krishnaiah, who was lynched by a mob in 1994. He was serving a life sentence before being released in April 2023 following a change in Bihar's prison remission rules. The top court's ruling came on a petition filed by G. Krishnaiah's wife, Uma Devi Krishnaiah, challenging the Bihar government's decision that paved the way for Anand Mohan's early release.
