title: Parliament Session Resumes Next Week; Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha To Meet On Different Dates, check Here
description: Parliament is set to reconvene, with the Lok Sabha scheduled to meet on November 30 and the Rajya Sabha on December 2. Kiren Rijiju said the sittings may conclude on December 3, depending on government business.
author: Swastika Sruti
content:
Parliament Session Resumes Next Week; Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha To Meet On Different Dates, check Here
The Parliament is all set to resume its proceedings next week. Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju announced that the government has asked the Lok Sabha to reconvene on Monday, November 30, while the Rajya Sabha has been requested to meet on Wednesday, December 2.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
The proposed sittings will continue the proceedings of Parliament's Monsoon Session. According to Rijiju, both Houses may conclude their sittings on December 3, depending on the business scheduled.
Lok Sabha And Rajya Sabha To Resume On Different Dates
In a post on X, Rijiju said the government had approached Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla with a request to reconvene the lower House on November 30.
The Centre has also requested Rajya Sabha Chairman CP Radhakrishnan to call a sitting of the upper House on December 2.
 The Government has requested Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha and Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha to reconvene Lok Sabha on Monday, 30th November, 2026 and Rajya Sabha on Wednesday, 2nd December, 2026 respectively to transact essential Government Business. Subject to exigencies of the Business, the sitting of both Houses may conclude on 3rd December, 2026.
— Kiren Rijiju (@KirenRijiju) November 26, 2026
The two Houses will therefore resume proceedings on separate dates as Parliament takes up the pending government business.
Rijiju said the sittings have been requested to conduct essential government business. However, the final schedule will depend on the work taken up by the two Houses.
"Subject to exigencies of the Business, the sitting of both Houses may conclude on 3rd December, 2026," he said.

title: West Bengal SIR Row: Newborn Denied Birth Certificate After Father's Name Is Deleted From Voter List
description: A two-month-old girl in Cooch Behar, West Bengal, is yet to receive her birth certificate after her father, Abdul Habib, was allegedly deleted from the voter list during the SIR exercise. The issue has triggered a political row involving the BJP, Congress and TMC.
author: PTI
content:
West Bengal SIR Row: Newborn Denied Birth Certificate After Father's Name Is Deleted From Voter List
A two-month-old girl in West Bengal's Cooch Behar district is yet to receive her birth certificate, with her family alleging that the registration process has been stalled after her father's name was deleted from the electoral rolls during the ongoing SIR exercise.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
The family claimed that the local gram panchayat has refused to issue a residency certificate to the father, Abdul Habib, following his exclusion from the voter list, leaving them unable to complete the registration process for the child born on September 8 at Dinhata Sub-Divisional Hospital.
Habib, a resident of Khatamari village under Chowdhurihat gram panchayat in Dinhata-II block, said his repeated visits to government offices had failed to resolve the matter. The absence of an elected pradhan in the panchayat has further compounded his difficulties, he alleged.
He was advised to approach the local MLA after failing to obtain the certificate. Habib has also challenged the deletion of his name before the SIR appellate tribunal but is yet to receive a hearing notice. Questioning why his electoral status should affect his daughter's birth registration, Habib pointed out that his wife, Amina Khatun, remains on the voter list.
The family also possesses the birth certificates of both parents and a copy of the 2002 electoral rolls bearing his father's name, he said. The incident has triggered a political confrontation in the district. The BJP asked Habib to pursue the matter through the appellate tribunal, while the Congress and the Trinamool Congress criticised the alleged hardships faced by families following the SIR exercise.
Cooch Behar BJP district president Abhijit Barman said Habib should challenge the deletion of his name before the appellate tribunal, expressing confidence that the matter would be resolved through the appropriate legal process. "If he is a genuine voter, his name will be restored after the tribunal examines his case.
He should approach the tribunal and file an appeal. If he is a genuine resident, there is no reason for him to worry about obtaining the birth certificate," Barman said. Congress district president Biswajit Sarkar alleged that the SIR exercise resulted in the exclusion of genuine voters, creating difficulties that now affect their families as well.
Describing Habib as a member of the local Muslim Rajbanshi community, Sarkar claimed that indigenous residents were being unfairly portrayed as outsiders. "Several genuine voters have been dropped from the electoral rolls, leaving their families to face serious difficulties. The problem has now reached newborns, who are reportedly unable to get their births registered. This is a serious issue in Cooch Behar, and we will continue our agitation until the names of eligible citizens are restored," Sarkar said.
He further alleged that the deletions were part of a wider attempt to deprive genuine voters of their electoral rights and said the Congress would continue to pursue the matter through protests and legal channels. Trinamool Congress MLA Kunal Ghosh also criticised the situation and called for intervention by both the state and central governments. "This is a matter of serious concern.
A newborn is being caught up in this controversy, and similar complaints are coming from different parts of the state. The state and the Centre must take cognisance of the situation and ensure that ordinary citizens are not subjected to such harassment," Ghosh said. He added that any discrepancies in the father's documents should be examined separately and should not be allowed to hold up the registration of the child's birth.
Dinhata-II Block Development Officer Lhamu Y Wangdi said the administration would look into the family's complaint. The case has added another dimension to the political controversy surrounding the SIR exercise in West Bengal, where allegations of genuine voters being excluded have become a major point of contention between the BJP and opposition parties. For Habib's family, however, the immediate battle is to secure a birth certificate for their daughter, more than two months after her birth.

title: Maharashtra's 2,500 MW RTC Tender Offers New Model to Turn Solar Surplus into Firm Power
description: Maharashtra's 2,500 MW RTC renewable procurement converts 5,000 MW of non-firm solar into firm power via a 25-year tariff-based tender, enabling reliable 24/7 electricity.
author: Oneindia Staff
content:
Maharashtra's 2,500 MW RTC Tender Offers New Model to Turn Solar Surplus into Firm Power
Maharashtra launches a 2,500 MW round-the-clock renewable power tender, converting 5,000 MW of non-firm solar into firm power through a 25-year tariff-based regime. Adani Power led the bids, with MERC approving a fixed Rs 5.90 per unit tariff to bolster reliable, greener electricity without dedicated generation assets.
Maharashtra is pioneering a new model of renewable energy procurement that aims to convert surplus daytime solar generation into reliable Round-the-Clock (RTC) electricity. The model addresses a growing challenge for power distribution utilities as renewable capacity expands.
According to people with knowledge of the matter, the Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co Ltd (MSEDCL) floated a tender earlier this year to procure 2,500 MW of RTC renewable power for 25 years. The procurement was carried out through tariff-based competitive bidding and an e-reverse auction.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
The tender effectively converted 5,000 MW of non-firm solar capacity into 2,500 MW of firm power by combining renewable energy with other generation sources and storage, the people said.
The Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) described the arrangement as "unique and bespoke". It said the arrangement would enable MSEDCL to "effectively utilise and convert the 5,000 MW of non-firm solar power...into a firm source of power".
No dedicated generation assets required for bidders
Unlike conventional power procurement contracts, this supply-based arrangement does not require bidders to own dedicated generation assets. Suppliers can source electricity from multiple generators and technologies, but must meet stringent annual, monthly and peak-hour supply obligations. These include a minimum 51 per cent traceable renewable energy component.
The model shifts the responsibility for sourcing, scheduling and balancing power to suppliers, while MSEDCL retains control over how the procured electricity is deployed.
Competitive tariff for consumers
Consumer economics are central to the arrangement. MERC noted that the tariff of Rs 5.90 per unit discovered by MSEDCL compares favourably with levelised tariffs of Rs 6.31-8.90 per unit for recent long-term thermal power procurement. The tariff is fixed for the 25-year power purchase agreement, and suppliers bear the risk of fluctuations in input power costs.
Adani Power wins the contract
Four bidders offered a combined 6,250 MW. Adani Power Limited (APL) won the contract after quoting Rs 6.30 per kWh initially and securing the lowest tariff in the e-reverse auction. It was followed by Lalitpur Power Generation Company (Rs 6.34 per kWh), MB Power (Rs 6.48 per kWh) and Sterlite Grid 42 (Rs 9.50 per kWh).
APL has received the Letter of Award (LOA), and MERC has adopted the Rs 5.90 per kWh tariff, the people said. The tender also imposes substantial delivery obligations, with penalties for non-performance reaching up to 400 per cent of the applicable tariff in specified cases. MERC described the bidding process as "fair, transparent, and competitive", citing the substantial market response.
Addressing a growing imbalance in the power market
The model seeks to address a growing imbalance in India's electricity market: solar generation peaks during daylight hours, while demand continues after sunset. Better use of surplus solar power could reduce renewable energy curtailment, improve utilisation of the transmission network and limit the inefficient backing down of thermal power plants.
West Bengal follows with similar procurement
The approach is beginning to find traction elsewhere. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd (WBSEDCL) has recently concluded a similar 2,500 MW RTC procurement, comprising 1,750 MW and a 750 MW greenshoe option. Its contract provides for a first-year tariff with subsequent escalation linked to the Wholesale Price Index (WPI), the people said.
The two procurements could provide a template for other states seeking to integrate larger volumes of renewable energy without compromising supply reliability or adding to the burden of under-utilised conventional generation assets.
A shift towards dependable green power
The broader significance lies in a shift in renewable power procurement, from buying intermittent green electricity to securing dependable, round-the-clock power with a substantial renewable component. As India's solar capacity expands, such arrangements could become increasingly important in balancing clean-energy ambitions with the need for reliable and affordable electricity.

title: Pune court attack: Six held, remanded in police custody till December 2; victim critical

Pune court attack: Six held, remanded in police custody till Dec 2; victim critical

Police have identified nine accused in the case, including a minor, while two more persons have been taken into custody and will be produced before a court on Friday, Pune Police Commissioner Amitesh Kumar said
The police had sought 10 days of custody for the six arrested accused to investigate the attack. File Pic/PTI
Six persons have been so far arrested in connection with the brutal attack on a 35-year-old murder accused outside Pune's Shivajinagar court premises, police said, adding that they have been remanded in police custody till December 2, reported the PTI.

title: Mumbai leopard sightings: Leopard spotted at residential society in Mumbai's Goregaon trapped by forest officials
description: Angry wildlife enthusiasts demand accountability from authorities over trapping of big cat in Goregaon despite absence of human-wildlife conflict
author: Ranjeet Jadhav
content:
Home / Mumbai / Mumbai News / Article /
Leopard spotted at residential society in Mumbai's Goregaon trapped, wildlife enthusiasts demand accountability
Updated On: 26 November, 2026 10:40 PM IST | Mumbai | Ranjeet Jadhav
Angry wildlife enthusiasts demand accountability from authorities over trapping of big cat in Goregaon despite absence of human-wildlife conflict
The leopard that was trapped by the Maharashtra Forest Department in Goregaon East. Pics/By Special Arrangement
News of a leopard being trapped by Maharashtra Forest Department in Dindoshi, Goregaon East in the early hours of Thursday has triggered strong reactions from nature lovers and wildlife enthusiasts, who questioned the rationale behind the operation in the absence of any reported human-wildlife conflict. A strongly worded message questioning the decision to let the animal walk into a cage near Samata Sankalp Society, close to Ganesh Mandir, soon went viral on WhatsApp groups dedicated to wildlife, nature, and conservation, with members expressing their anger and demanding accountability from the authorities, warning that treating mere sightings as a reason to trap leopards could set a dangerous precedent and undermine efforts to promote coexistence with wildlife.
“Today it’s a leopard in Goregaon East. Tomorrow, will every leopard sighting around SGNP result in a cage? Wildlife lovers must demand answers. A sighting is not a conflict. Coexistence cannot be replaced by unnecessary trapping. Are we moving towards a future where every leopard sighting will end with the animal being trapped?” read the WhatsApp message.

title: ‘I have no faith in astrology’: How Nehru stood by January 26 in a 1949 letter to Rajendra Prasad
description: Before The Constitution Was Adopted, Rajendra Prasad Suggested Quietly Exploring A More Auspicious Date For It To Take Effect. Nehru Warned That Changing January 26 Would Provoke A 'bitter Controversy'
author: Our Web Desk, PTI
content:
Two months before the Constituent Assembly adopted India’s Constitution, Rajendra Prasad wrote to Jawaharlal Nehru from Pilani with a question: should they look for a more auspicious date than January 26 for it to come into force? Nehru’s reply, sent from New Delhi on September 27, 1949, was blunt.
“I am afraid I have no faith in astrology and certainly I should not like to fix up national programmes in accordance with the dictates of astrologers,” Nehru wrote in the letter accessed by PTI.
Prasad, then president of the Constituent Assembly, had written two days earlier, enclosing a letter from someone he said he did not know. The writer considered January 26 a “very unauspicious day” for inaugurating the Constitution and had suggested choosing another date.
Prasad recalled that August 15, 1947, had been fixed for the transfer of power without consulting astrologers. Some had predicted trouble once the date was announced, he wrote, but the leadership had stuck with it. This time, he wondered whether elected representatives ought to take people’s beliefs into account.
“But when we act not in an individual capacity but as representatives of millions and millions of men and women who have that faith, it may not be improper to consider their feelings in the matter, particularly when no loss may be apprehended by doing so,” Prasad wrote.
He recognised the significance of January 26 and suggested making discreet inquiries, “unofficially and without making a parade of it”, about the most auspicious day and time.
Nehru doubted that the letter writer spoke for millions. Changing the date, he said, would take a great deal of explanation, would reflect poorly on the country and could anger many in India. If the belief really was that widespread, he wrote, the leadership could “either combat this delusion, if we consider it so, or allow others, who believe in astrology, to take charge of the destiny of the nation”.
The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on November 26, 1949, after nearly three years of deliberations. It came into force on January 26, 1950, honouring the date in 1930 when the Congress marked Independence Day following its call for Purna Swaraj, or complete independence.
November 26 is now observed as Constitution Day, or Samvidhan Divas. Prasad went on to become independent India’s first President. Nehru was its first prime minister.

title: Union Cabinet to take up women's quota bill on Friday as Centre plans Parliament session next week
description: The Government’s Decision To Seek The Reconvening Of Parliament Also Comes After The Monsoon Session Remained Unprorogued For More Than 100 Days Following Its Adjournment Sine Die On August 13
author: Our Web Desk, PTI
content:
The government has convened an important meeting of the Union Cabinet on Friday afternoon, where the delimitation-linked women's quota bill will be taken up ahead of the special sitting of the Lok Sabha on November 30, according to sources.
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju said on Thursday that the Union government proposed reconvening Parliament from November 30 to December 2 to transact essential government business amid speculation over the women's reservation and delimitation bills.
Rijiju said the government had requested the Lok Sabha Speaker and Rajya Sabha Chairman to reconvene the two Houses — the Lok Sabha on Monday, November 30, and the Rajya Sabha on Wednesday, December 2. Subject to the exigencies of government business, the sittings of both Houses may conclude on December 3, he said in a post on X.
Sources said the Lok Sabha was likely to meet for two days, followed by two days of proceedings in the Rajya Sabha.
The development comes on a day Prime Minister Narendra Modi asserted that no force can stop the delivery of justice to women and blamed "one opposition party" for the defeat in Parliament of the delimitation-linked Constitution amendment bill, giving 33 per cent reservation to women.
In a signed article that appeared in major newspapers on Thursday, Modi said, "The journey of our Constitution would be incomplete without recognising the remarkable women who helped shape it. But what happened earlier this year should fill our hearts with shame."
The prime minister said the legislation aimed at giving women adequate representation in legislative bodies was disallowed from being passed by one opposition party, once again showing its “disdain for constitutional values”.
"I assure the 'Nari Shakti' of India that no force can prevent us from ensuring that justice is done to them," he said.
The proposed amendment would raise the Lok Sabha’s strength from 543 seats to a maximum of 850 through delimitation. The aim is to implement 33 per cent reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies ahead of the 2029 general election.
Southern states have raised concerns that delimitation could reduce their share of Lok Sabha seats. The government is understood to be considering a 50 per cent increase in seats for every state. Another option is to retain the existing distribution of seats among states, which is based on the 1971 Census. No final decision has been taken.
The government’s decision to seek the reconvening of Parliament also comes after the Monsoon Session remained unprorogued for more than 100 days following its adjournment sine die on August 13. The unusual gap had fuelled speculation that the government could reconvene the House at short notice to take up the delimitation package.
In a post on X, Congress MP Manish Tewari said the request “mocks the institution of Parliament”, while adding that it was time for the Winter Session to convene. To be sure, the government had not prorogued the Monsoon Session, which concluded on August 13.
Therefore, the session remains technically alive and under Rule 15 of the Lok Sabha rules and corresponding Rajya Sabha rules, the Speaker or Chairman can call a sitting at any time without the President summoning a fresh session.
Tewari added, “A Special Session is a mechanism for convening during the inter-session period. It can and should not become a substitute for a regular winter session.” He further said, “Why not just convene a regular winter session and the government can if the government chooses too, it can always regurgitate defeated legislation.”
Congress general secretary (communications) Jairam Ramesh said that on the evening of Ambedkar Jayanti on April 14, 2026, the Modi government had made the delimitation bills public, which met their "well-deserved" fate on the night of April 17.
"Now on Constitution Day, after 105 days of Operation Lotus, the Modi government announces a special session, hoping that it will get its super-tainted two-thirds majority to pass a Constitution amendment bill," Ramesh said on X.
Can there be a greater insult to and assault on the Constitution, he asked.
"The fight is on," Ramesh asserted.
Tagging Ramesh's post, Congress MP Shashi Tharoor said on X, "Absolutely. The fight is on -- a fight to save Indian democracy, to protect India's unity and to save our Parliament's integrity."
Meanwhile, CPI(M)'s Brittas claimed that the “real expenditure” of the session would be “humongous.” He further accused the government of trying to “manufacture a majority.” “A majority manufactured through political manipulation is not a mandate. It is a mockery of democracy,” Brittas said. He alleged that India's electoral future was being “reshaped”, while terming the special sitting as “the saddest chapter in the history of Indian democracy.”

title: Maharashtra to offer 1 lakh autorickshaws to farmers in drought-hit areas over five years
description: Those Eligible, Whose Names Had Been Forwarded To The State Government By District Collectors Could Apply At Their Respective Regional Transport Offices, The Minister Says
author: PTI
content:
Small and marginal farmers in Maharashtra’s drought-hit talukas will be able to apply for subsidised passenger autorickshaws under a scheme aimed at giving them a source of income alongside farming. The state plans to distribute one lakh vehicles over five years, with a subsidy covering a tenth of the cost and loans financing the rest.
Transport minister Pratap Sarnaik announced the scheme on Thursday at the transport commissioner’s office in Bandra. He said 20,000 autorickshaws would be distributed annually from 2027 to 2031 under the Anathanchaa Nath Dushkalgrast Shetkari Rickshaw Sanman Yojana.
Nationalised banks, scheduled banks and other financial institutions would finance the remaining 90 per cent of the vehicle cost, Sarnaik said. The Dharmaveer Anand Dighe Maharashtra Passenger Transport Workers Welfare Board would facilitate the loans.
“The scheme will cover eligible farmers from more than 310 drought-affected talukas across the state. The beneficiaries will be selected through a lottery similar to the Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Authority (MHADA) draw,” he said.
Beneficiaries would have to pay Rs 800 to become members of the board, Sarnaik added.
“The board has also decided to propose a waiver of around Rs 23,500 to Rs 24,000 in fees for licences and permits. Licences, badges and permits would be provided free of cost under the scheme. The proposal will be sent to the state government for approval,” Sarnaik said.
The first autorickshaws would be handed over to selected beneficiaries on February 9, 2027, to coincide with deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde’s birthday, he said. Sarnaik is part of the Shinde-led Shiv Sena.
Eligible farmers whose names had been forwarded to the state government by district collectors could apply at their respective Regional Transport Offices (RTOs), the minister said. Beneficiaries would be allowed to operate their autorickshaws anywhere in the district in which their taluka falls.
The scheme would initially cover CNG- and LPG-run autorickshaws. Sarnaik cited limited access to electricity and charging infrastructure in remote and tribal areas, particularly in districts such as Gadchiroli and Chandrapur.
“Electric autorickshaws are also significantly more expensive, making the loan instalments unaffordable for small and marginal farmers. The government may consider switching to electric vehicles in the future,” he said.
Sarnaik said the scheme aimed to help farmers earn an additional Rs 1,000 to Rs 2,000 a day by operating the vehicles alongside farming.
How farmers will be selected
The first-year target is to provide autorickshaws to 20,000 eligible farmers across 310 drought-affected talukas, with an average allocation of around 60 vehicles per taluka. If a taluka has fewer eligible applicants than its allocation, the remaining vehicles will go to beneficiaries in other talukas in the same district.
The welfare board will invite applications through advertisements. It will scrutinise documents, draw up a final list of eligible applicants and select beneficiaries through a computerised lottery.
The selected applications will then go to banks for loan approval. Once the bank sanctions a loan covering 90 per cent of the cost, the board will release the 10 per cent subsidy. The vehicle cost will be paid directly to authorised dealers.
Applicants must be small or marginal farmers from drought-affected areas and provide proof of agricultural land ownership. They must hold a valid driving licence or meet the requirements to obtain one and satisfy the lender’s loan conditions. Farmers who have already benefited from a similar government scheme are ineligible.

title: Sonia Gandhi's book 'Belonging' sheds light on her turbulent journey in Indian politics
description: Sonia Gandhi's memoir revisits love, loss and political inheritance, offering a deeply personal defence of her family and its legacy.
author: Soutik Biswas
content:
'They will kill you too': Sonia Gandhi's turbulent journey in Indian politics
- Published
On the morning of 31 October 1984, Sonia Gandhi was a young wife and mother, living in the prime minister's residence in Delhi. She was about to take a bath when she heard shots ring out in the garden.
Her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, India's prime minister, had just left for her office in an adjoining building. Moments later, she would be assassinated by two of her Sikh bodyguards, in retaliation for the Indian army's storming of the Golden Temple in Amritsar, Sikhism's holiest shrine, earlier that year.
The sound was like firecrackers, but "different". The children's nanny came pounding on the bathroom door, hysterical, pointing towards the garden.
Sonia ran towards the path. A white Ambassador car was moving slowly towards her. Inside, Indira lay covered in blood, her sari stained, her eyes open, her face wearing what Sonia remembered as a look of surprise.
"Mummy, Mummy," she tried to say. No words came. At the hospital, she waited for hours before a doctor's shake of the head told her what she feared.
The ordeal did not end there. Rajiv Gandhi, her husband and the elder son of Indira Gandhi, summoned from a rally in West Bengal, arrived to tell her that party leaders wanted him to become prime minister.
Sonia's response was fury and terror. "They will kill you; they will kill you, too!" she pleaded. Rajiv replied: "They will kill me anyway." That evening, as Indira's body lay at home, Rajiv was sworn in.
It is one of the most searing passages in Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi's new memoir: private devastation unfolding alongside the pressures of public life.
The woman who had largely stayed away from politics was now married to India's prime minister, and would eventually find herself at the head of the Congress party, leading it through two general election victories and becoming one of the country's most consequential political figures.
The passage also foreshadows another devastating loss. In 1991, Rajiv himself was assassinated.
For Sonia, the years that followed were marked by retreat.
At 19, a young woman from a small Italian town, she had met Rajiv, an Indian student, in England. Their relationship took her into a new country and family, and a close bond with Indira followed. India became home through her husband and her mother-in-law.
After Rajiv's killing, even the public appearances required by the memorial trusts she headed became an ordeal. Before speeches, she feared tears would overwhelm her.
When the Dalai Lama asked whether she felt vengeful towards her husband's killers, she answered, "No, I don't," and burst into sobs. Slowly, she writes, Rajiv became "a presence within me rather than a piercing absence".
But grief returned at family milestones. At her son Rahul's Cambridge graduation in 1995, she and her children were overcome by the thought of how proud Rajiv would have been.
Politics, meanwhile, was closing in. The Congress party, the political vehicle of her husband's family for generations, was losing cohesion and electoral ground. Senior leaders were defecting, and the calls for Sonia to step in were growing louder.
She initially refused. She writes she had seen politics through Rajiv: its achievements, but also its "ambition and greed, hypocrisy and treachery". "I'd always disliked politics," she writes. It had taken first her mother-in-law, then "the love of my life, my children's father".
Yet the party's decline began to feel personal. Walking past photographs of Indira and Rajiv, she was seized by "a mixture of pain and guilt". She feared that the forces they had fought to "protect India's pluralistic ethos" were gaining ground: a rising Hindu nationalism that, in her view, threatened the "secular and pluralistic vision" of India they had sought to defend.
Congress leaders argued that without her, the party could splinter, leaving little to resist communal politics. The family name, she believed, carried an appeal beyond religion, caste, language and region. This, she says, was "the most compelling argument".
Her doubts were also about her own credentials. How could an outsider occupy a position held by two formidable figures? At home, Rahul and Priyanka feared losing their mother as they had lost their grandmother and father. Before a New Year holiday, they extracted a promise: "Don't you do anything crazy while we're away."
The "answer", she says, came through the Bhagavad Gita. Though not religious in adult life, Sonia arranged private lessons with a Sanskrit scholar in January 1997. They read the text verse by verse. She writes that its central message – to perform one's dharma, or duty, without attachment to the fruits of one's actions – eventually resolved her inner conflict.
"I had the answer to my own doubts and questions. I had to step out and go where my duty called. And I did."
The memoir's most dramatic political scene, however, comes seven years later, after Congress's 2004 election victory. Sonia had led the party's campaign.
Sonia goes with Manmohan Singh to meet India's president at the presidential palace in Delhi and formally stake the Congress-led alliance's claim to form a government. Everyone assumes she will become prime minister. She says nothing.
At home, she tells a senior aide she intends to refuse. Party workers gather at the gates; senior colleagues demand a meeting.
"You fought the election, you led us," says one. "People believed in you. How can you let them down like this? Our workers will revolt. You think they'll accept another leader?"
Alliance leaders arrive to persuade her. They surround her, she recalls, and one insists: "We will not take no for an answer." Overwhelmed, she murmurs "Theek hai" - all right. They take it as consent and begin congratulating her.
Her children are appalled, she writes. Rahul storms in: "You said yes?" Her daughter Priyanka urges her not to be forced into a decision.
Sonia writes she spends a long night arguing with herself, friends and family. The risk is not merely personal. She believes the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) would continue to exploit her foreign birth and that accepting office would allow the controversy to "create havoc" and hurt the country. By morning she is clear. "I've made up my mind. I'm going to stick to my stand," she tells Rahul.
She chooses Singh, a trained economist and a party member, instead, describing him as a man "above reproach", with a "deep and consummate understanding of governance".
The book is at its most revealing when it turns from family memory to the India she believes has been lost.
Sonia says that when she entered public life there was "a certain decency and decorum in parliamentary politics".
Political attacks and harsh words were not new, but she sees a sharper appetite among those in power "to belittle and torment those who differ from them, to intimidate those they perceive as opponents". It is, she says, part of a wider international drift towards "a heartlessness that accompanies authoritarian regimes".
Her portrait of prime minister Narendra Modi of the Hindu nationalist BJP is unusually direct.
The two have had "practically no real contact", she writes, beyond formal greetings at parliamentary gatherings and occasional exchanges - "Theek hain, aap?" ("Are you all right?") - when she returned from hospital. "He tends to look away," she says, "avoiding eye contact."
Modi's idea of India, she writes, was shaped by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and "affirmed a fundamentalism in which his faith and culture superseded all others". His is an India of "hierarchy, order, and control"; hers is "an India against hegemony", standing for "inclusiveness, secularism, and social justice".
There is a striking concession amid the polemic - she says she understood Modi's "discomfort with the ruling elite of our times".
Sonia says she felt uneasy in Delhi's privileged drawing rooms, where political conversation seemed "very far removed from the reality of India".
Modi's origins, she writes, "may not be as humble as his PR team" suggests, but he "had certainly worked his way to power within the RSS from an underprivileged world". It is a rare acknowledgement of the social distance between the Congress establishment and the electorate Modi came to represent.
The memoir also offers some glimpses of Sonia's encounters with world leaders.
She remembers Vladimir Putin as an "engaging personality" who took her on a boat ride in St Petersburg, pointing out monuments along the way. She says she was impressed by his grasp of geopolitics and his "determination to restore Russia to its former powerful status" - "long before the Ukraine war, a different era".
A more amusing encounter involved France's Nicolas Sarkozy, who arrived in India in 2008 without his then partner Carla Bruni because they were unmarried.
At a state banquet, the Indian vice-president's wife cheerfully grilled him about when he planned to marry her, whether he missed her and whether a date had been fixed. Sarkozy obligingly answered her questions while messaging Bruni on his phone.
Belonging is not a neutral history. The Bofors gun scandal, which badly damaged Rajiv Gandhi's government and dogged the family for decades, gets a relatively brief treatment.
The 502-page memoir is less forthcoming about the less flattering aspects of Congress's own record. Sonia has much to say about political corruption, hypocrisy and the decline of public standards under her opponents, but largely sidesteps the culture of patronage, cronyism and corruption that dogged Congress during its years in power. There is little reckoning, either, with the party's own share of responsibility for the erosion of public trust.
She is at pains to defend the political inheritance of her husband and mother-in-law, even as the party they built has suffered a prolonged decline. The story she tells is as much about the costs of carrying that inheritance as it is about a woman who says she never wanted the life she ended up leading.
That gives the memoir's final pages an unmistakable melancholy. Sonia, 79, is now a member of the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of parliament. Rahul, 55, is a four-term MP and leader of the opposition; Priyanka, 53, is also a member of parliament.
Sonia says the challenge was to remain faithful to "a just and humane society", through pain and loss, victory and defeat, and the manoeuvring that politics demands. But she ends not with triumph, nor even with the assurance that history will vindicate her.
"At this moment it seems to me that, although I tried my best, I didn't succeed in beating back the forces I'd set out to fight."

title: Agniveer: Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?
description: India has softened its recruitment scheme, giving young soldiers a longer military stint and another shot at permanent service.
author: Nikita Yadav
content:
Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?
- Published
For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country.
In 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a new reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years. Only a quarter would be allowed to stay on permanently. The rest would return to civilian life with a lump-sum payment, but without the pension and other benefits that had long made military service an attractive career.
Now, as the first batch of recruits prepares to complete its four-year term, the government is offering them a chance to stay longer, in a significant shift in a policy that has been fiercely debated since its introduction.
On 4 November, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani announced that recruits who failed to secure permanent positions under the Agnipath, or "path of fire", programme would be offered another two years of service at higher pay. They would then get a second opportunity to join the regular forces, provided they met the selection criteria.
Gen Subramani said the decision followed feedback from the forces and insisted that Agnipath would continue.
But the timing is significant. More than 18,300 recruits from the first batch are due to complete their initial tenure by the end of 2026. Officials say the new arrangement will be offered to more than 300,000 Agniveers - as recruits under the scheme are known - currently serving across the army, navy and air force.
Whether future batches will also be covered remains unclear. The BBC has contacted the defence ministry for clarification.
The ministry has defended , externalAgnipath, saying internal assessments found the recruits to be physically fit, motivated and technologically adaptable. It also said the scheme had widened recruitment across districts and made the process more standardised.
But the extension has brought renewed attention to the trade-offs at the heart of the policy - and whether its original ambitions were realistic.
When the government introduced Agnipath, it argued the scheme would reduce the average age of the armed forces, lower long-term salary and pension costs and create a younger, more technologically adaptable fighting force.
But military experts and opposition leaders have questioned whether a four-year contract could replace what had traditionally been a coveted, long-term career in the armed forces.
"Being a soldier in the armed forces was a chance for these young men to make a life for themselves, to get their families out of poor or lower-middle-income conditions," says retired Maj Gen Yash Mor, a vocal critic of the scheme.
These concerns were also amplified by the timing of Agnipath's launch. Recruitment had been suspended for nearly two years during the Covid pandemic, leaving thousands of aspirants waiting for vacancies to reopen.
The changes were greeted by massive protests across the country, with many saying the career path they had spent years preparing for had fundamentally changed.
This sentiment was felt most in states and cities that have traditionally been major recruitment hubs, where military service has been a family tradition for generations.
Kulbeer Singh Chaudhary, who runs a recruitment training institute in Dehradun city, says interest in joining the armed forces fell sharply and he stopped conducting Agniveer training batches.
The latest announcement, he hopes, would reverse that trend.
"The possibility of a longer engagement and eventual absorption into the forces may offer young candidates greater assurance," he says.
The changes also come at a time when the armed forces are facing personnel shortages. In November last year, The Indian Express reported, external that the army alone faced a shortfall of nearly 180,000 soldiers and was considering increasing recruitment.
But the debate over Agnipath goes beyond what happens to recruits after four years. Critics also question whether that is enough time to turn them into experienced soldiers.
Sanjiv Krishan Sood, a former additional director general of the Border Security Force, has argued, external that the shorter training period is particularly problematic for technical roles requiring specialised skills.
Retired Maj Gen Mor says military effectiveness depends on experience and trust built over years.
"It takes eight-to-nine years to turn a raw recruit into a dependable, seasoned soldier - someone capable of handling a tank crew, an artillery gun crew or a small detachment," he says.
"Over those years, a soldier develops the ethos, camaraderie, brotherhood and fighting spirit that bind a unit together. These qualities cannot be built overnight."
Sood says the additional two years could help improve recruits' skills, particularly in handling specialised equipment.
Senior military leaders have also welcomed the extension. Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav told news agency ANI, external it would allow the forces to retain trained personnel for longer.
But the change could create fresh challenges within military units.
Regular soldiers, Agniveers on four-year contracts and those serving an additional two years could find themselves working alongside one another despite differences in pay, promotion prospects and post-service benefits.
Experts warn that these disparities could affect unit cohesion.
There is also the question of whether the changes will undermine one of the government's central objectives: reducing spending. Almost half of India's defence budget, external goes towards salaries and pensions, leaving less money for modernisation and new equipment.
By limiting the number of personnel eligible for long-term benefits, Agnipath was expected to ease that burden. But critics argue that savings should not come at the expense of military effectiveness.
"We are not against making changes, but there are ways and means to go about it," says Mor, adding that the government could instead reduce annual recruitment while retaining soldiers for longer periods.
He also points to India's tense borders with Pakistan and China, where troops remain deployed year-round, placing sustained demands on manpower and operational experience.
Retired Major-General Birender Singh Dhanoa, meanwhile, questions whether shorter service makes financial sense when the military is investing in training to operate increasingly sophisticated equipment.
"The amount of time it takes to train, and the financial outlay for training, is much higher for modern equipment. So shouldn't you get the best bang for your buck?" he asks.
Many retired officers had proposed a different approach when the scheme was announced, he says.
"We suggested that if you want to reduce your financial burden, you increase the terms and conditions of service. Take these guys for eight-or-nine years and retain a larger number after that."
The announcement also comes at a politically sensitive time. Elections are due soon in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - states that have traditionally supplied large numbers of soldiers and where military recruitment remains an important source of employment.
The opposition Congress party has called the revision a "u-turn", alleging that the government is responding to fears of losing votes.
For young recruits approaching the end of their contracts, the changes offer some reassurance, but few guarantees. Two more years of service could mean more money, greater experience and another chance at a permanent career.
But for many, it also means putting their futures on hold, without knowing whether they will eventually be allowed to stay.

title: CJP: India’s protesters face government crackdown after summer victory
description: A new wave of youth dissent swept India this summer, fuelled by frustration and irreverent online satire.
author: Azadeh Moshiri
content:
After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
- Published
Cheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.
One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."
Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained.
The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire.
The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".
This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests.
But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.
"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."
The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online.
"It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations.
"The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."
Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.
In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.
Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.
Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.
His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".
"We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.
Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.
Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.
CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar.
The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.
Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders.
"We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.
Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect.
"A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.
The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.
"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."
The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.
Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".
Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.
Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress.
"Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.
They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.
Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.
CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.
Yet dissent has not been stamped out.
Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities.
CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation.
When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling.
"I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."

title: 4 Constitution amendments Modi wants GenZ to study, from curbs on free speech to Emergency powers
description: PM Modi also criticised “repeated misuse” of Article 356 of the Constitution, which allows the President to impose President’s Rule in a state when constitutional machinery fails.
author: Apoorva Mandhani
content:
New Delhi: The first amendment to the Indian Constitution was to “stifle public opposition”, and the 38th and 39th amendments should be studied by the youngsters to understand “what a power-hungry and anti-constitutional leadership can do”, Prime Minister Narendra Modi wrote in an op-ed on Constitution Day on Thursday.
The op-ed was published on his website narendramodi.in as well as various newspapers, to mark Constitution Day or Samvidhan Divas, commemorating the day the Constituent Assembly adopted the Indian Constitution on 26 November 1949.
The article begins by listing down the manner in which the government in the last 12 years has contributed to “strengthening our Constitution”. However, the mood of the op-ed turns sombre quickly, when PM Modi feels “compelled” to share “another reality”.
“There have been occasions in our history when those entrusted with upholding the Constitution chose to weaken it. Ironically, they are the same people who had the opportunity to govern India for five decades,” he wrote.
He then talks about the first amendment to the Constitution, passed in 1951, and the 38th, 39th and 42nd amendments passed during the Emergency.
“This year marks 75 years since the First Amendment of 1951, when a government that was not popularly elected used its majority in the Provisional Parliament to restrict fundamental freedoms. Its timing, barely months before India’s first general election, proves that it was intended to influence the electoral process and stifle public opposition. It is also 50 years since the 42nd Amendment at the height of the Emergency. This curtailed judicial review and fundamentally altered the balance of institutional powers. I would also urge youngsters to study the 38th and 39th Amendments to know what a power-hungry and anti-constitutional leadership can do,” he wrote.
What do these amendments say and why are they so controversial? ThePrint explains.
Why was the First Amendment introduced
The first amendment to the Indian Constitution is also one of its most controversial and polarising.
It was brought in by the Provisional Parliament, only 16 months after the Constitution was enforced. The reason was Supreme Court judgments in various cases, including Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras and Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi.
In the Romesh Thapar verdict passed in May 1950, the Supreme Court quashed the order issued by the Madras government banning communist magazine Cross Roads, edited and published by Romesh Thapar from Bombay. Thapar had asserted that the ban violated his freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
The apex court upheld Thapar’s challenge to the order, and struck down a provision of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949, observing that it was “void and unconstitutional”, since it authorised restrictions on a fundamental right wider than what was constitutionally permissible.
In the Brij Bhushan judgment passed on the same date on 26 May 1950, the Supreme Court quashed an order issued by the Chief Commissioner of Delhi, banning RSS weekly Organiser.
Concerned about the Supreme Court’s decisions, the Provisional Parliament introduced the first ever amendment to the Constitution of Article.
Article 19(2) of the Constitution, as it stood before this amendment, allowed the government to make laws relating to “libel, slander, defamation, contempt of court or any matter which offends against decency or morality or which undermines the security of, or tends to overthrow, the State”. In other words, the provision allowed the freedom of speech and expression to be restricted on these grounds.
The first amendment changed this. Passed in 16 days, it allowed the State to make a law that “imposes reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause in the interests of the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence”.
In effect, the amendment allowed the government to impose “reasonable restrictions” on certain grounds, including “public order”, “incitement to an offence” and “friendly relations with foreign states”. It has, therefore, been criticised for lowering the bar for the reasons on which the freedom of speech and expression can be curtailed.
Also Read: On Constitution Day, PM Modi targets opposition over defeat of women’s quota bill in LS
Why is the 42nd amendment called the ‘mini’ Constitution
The 42nd Constitutional amendment was by far, and still is, the most comprehensive of all the amendments. It amended the Preamble, 40 Articles and the Seventh Schedule, and added 14 new Articles. The magnitude of changes has earned the amendment the moniker, “mini” Constitution.
The amendment added the words “socialist” and “secular”, and added to the Constitution the fundamental duties that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Bharatiya Janata Party have often emphasised.
The delimitation exercise was also put on hold through this amendment. Through changes to Articles 81 and 82 of the Constitution, it effectively froze the number and boundaries of parliamentary constituencies or the delimitation exercise—based on the 1971 Census until the publication of the post-2000 Census. In 2001, the 84th Amendment to the Constitution extended the deadline from 2000 to 2026.
The amendment also made fundamental rights subservient to the Directive Principles of State Policy. It gave the Parliament unbridled powers to amend any part of the Constitution. It restricted the powers of the Supreme Court and high courts to strike down any laws that violated the Constitution. Through these changes, the amendment destabilised the separation of powers, tilting the scales in favour of the ruling central government.
The amendment also introduced changes to the Seventh Schedule, which deals with the division of the crucial lawmaking powers between the Centre and the states. It transferred five subjects—education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice—from the state list to the concurrent list. A new entry, 20A, was also added to the Concurrent list, adding population control and family planning as a subject.
Both Parliament and state governments can enact laws on the subjects listed under the concurrent list. However, according to Article 254, if there is a conflict between laws, the central law overrides the state law.
Provisions for establishing tribunals were also introduced, as were Articles 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), 43A (participation of workers in the management of industries), 48A (protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding of forests and wildlife), and 39(f) (protection of children and youth).
While subsequent amendments and court judgments overturned the amendments introduced by Indira Gandhi, other changes, including the fundamental duties and the changes made to the Preamble, despite periodic opposition, seem to have stood the test of time.
How the 38th and 39th amendments altered the balance of power
The 38th and 39th amendments to the Constitution were also introduced during the Emergency.
The 38th amendment, among other things, made the President’s decision to proclaim a national Emergency “final and conclusive”, keeping it outside the purview of even the courts. It also amended Article 356 of the Constitution, which allows the President to impose President’s Rule in a state when constitutional machinery fails. The amendment made the President’s satisfaction on the necessity of the order “final and conclusive” in this case as well.
In effect, it barred courts from questioning the national Emergency, President’s rule in States and financial emergency, and allowed multiple proclamations of National Emergency to be issued at the same time on different grounds.
The amendment also altered Article 359, which allows the President to suspend the right to approach a court for the enforcement of fundamental rights of the Constitution. The amendment allowed the State to make laws or take executive action which it could not have done under ordinary circumstances for violating the fundamental rights. It allowed the State to enact such laws while a Presidential order under Article 359(1) suspending the enforcement of fundamental rights was in force.
However, several of these amendments were overturned by the 44th amendment brought by the new Janata Party government.
The 39th Constitutional amendment barred Indian courts from scrutinizing election disputes involving the President, Vice President, Prime Minister, and Lok Sabha Speaker, through insertion of a new Article 329A, among other things.
However, in a judgment passed in November 1975, in Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain, the Supreme Court struck down certain provisions of Article 329A, and the entire provision as well as several other changes brought through the 39th amendment were removed through the 44th amendment.
‘Another troubling chapter’
Apart from the amendments, PM Modi also criticised “repeated misuse” of Article 356 of the Constitution, which allows the President to impose President’s Rule in a state when constitutional machinery fails.
Without naming the Congress party, he wrote, “The repeated misuse of Article 356 to dismiss elected state governments presents another troubling chapter. One party has the dubious record of imposing Article 356 almost a hundred times and one former Prime Minister has scored a half-century in this field.”
He then went on to take credit for the abrogation of Article 370 of the Constitution of India, and removal of Article 35A, asserting that the provisions “did not allow the full Constitution to be implemented in Jammu and Kashmir, thus trampling over the rights of SC, ST, OBC communities and women”.
He said that it was “only in 2019 that this historical wrong was corrected”.
(Edited by Anupama Yadav)

title: Delhi Police Crime Branch unit busts cyber slavery racket, rescues 164 foreign nationals from Noida
description: Among those rescued were 92 Indonesian nationals and 72 Malaysian nationals, who were allegedly lured to India with the promise of jobs.
author: Alisha Dutta
content:
New Delhi: The Delhi Police’s Crime Branch Thursday rescued 164 foreign nationals from a call centre in Noida as it busted what it called a major transnational ‘cyber slavery’ racket.
Among those rescued were 92 Indonesian nationals and 72 Malaysian nationals, who were allegedly lured to India with the promise of jobs.
The racket came to light when a foreign national wrote an email to the Crime Branch a week ago. “The foreign national who had come a month back, informed us that other foreign nationals are being held captive and made to commit cyber fraud in a call centre in Noida’s Sector 136,” said Joint Commissioner of Police (Crime Branch) Surender Kumar.
The complainant alleged he was lured to India with the promise of a tech job but when he landed in the country, his “managers” snatched his passport. “He was told that he had to commit digital fraud and when he protested that he would not engage in such criminal activities, he was abused,” said the Joint CP.
Told that around 60-65 foreign nationals were being held hostage as part of the racket, a police team conducted a raid at the call centre which allegedly belonged to a company called SKV Infratech. The team found 164 foreign nationals from Malaysia and Indonesia.
Those rescued fall in the age range of 19 and 22 years, and had been brought from Malaysia and Indonesia over the past four months, Joint CP Kumar said. “They were all promised well-paying jobs but were given phones, laptops, desktops and foreign SIM cards to carry out criminal activities. Initial probe has revealed that fraudulent online platforms, websites and APK-based applications including Zenttrix, Quantvoro and other similar platforms were being used.”
Online relationships, fake profiles
The modus operandi of the fraudsters allegedly involved creating fictitious female identities and online profiles to approach prospective victims through social media and other communication platforms. “The fraudsters developed online relationships, gained the confidence of victims and subsequently induced them to invest money through fraudulent trading and investment platforms,” Kumar said.
The police Thursday arrested one William alias Tan Guan Wei (25), a Malaysian national who was allegedly in-charge of bringing men from Malaysia and Indonesia. He has been booked under several sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and the IT Act.
Along with William, the police have identified two others—Sushil and Anil Kumar—both Indian nationals, who are currently absconding and believed to be abroad.
“We are currently trying to see if they (enslaved foreign nationals and the absconding Indian nationals suspected to be involved) are connected with any pre-registered cases. The Ministry of External Affairs has also reached out to the Malaysian and Indonesian governments to enable the process of their (rescued foreign nationals’) travel,” the officer said.
(Edited by Gitanjali Das)

title: UP with have Muslim, OBC deputy CMs is our alliance is voted to power, say Owaisi & Chandrashekhar Azad
description: Owaisi and Azad call BJP and RSS ‘enemies of the Constitution’ at Lucknow rally, also take aim at SP chief Akhilesh.
author: Prashant Srivastava
content:
Lucknow: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi and Azad Samaj Party (ASP) chief Chandrashekhar Azad announced Thursday that their alliance will have two deputy chief ministers, one Muslim and one OBC, if voted to power in Uttar Pradesh.
Chandrashekhar Azad, who has been named the chief ministerial candidate of the alliance—the Samajik Parivartan Morcha (SPM)—made the announcement alongwith Owaisi at a rally in Lucknow, where they launched a sharp attack on the BJP, RSS and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav.
At the rally held on Constitution Day, Owaisi accused the BJP and RSS of being enemies of the Constitution and urged people to protect it, saying it was a matter of life and death for Muslims, Dalits and weaker sections.
‘Modi, Yogi responsible for hatred spread in UP’
Uttar Pradesh had seen Thakur and Yadav dominance in the past, but the alliance wanted to bring people’s rule through the ballot, Owaisi said Thursday.
“Now Abdul will not just lay the carpet but will claim his share through votes and build his own leadership,” the AIMIM chief further said, adding that he would rather die than tolerate oppression.
He also took aim at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath: “I want to tell you that two people are responsible for the poison and hatred spread in this country and Uttar Pradesh: Narendra Modi and Yogi Adityanath.”
Owaisi said his alliance with Chandrashekhar Azad was a coming together of hearts and described Constitution Day as an occasion to remember those who framed the Constitution.
Referring to BR Ambedkar, Owaisi said people should neither be politically nor mentally enslaved and should instead develop their own leadership.
He said the RSS and Sangh Parivar were “enemies of the Constitution” and that the AIMIM-ASP alliance was prepared to make sacrifices to protect it. “If the Constitution is weakened or destroyed, it will become a question of life and death, particularly for Muslims, Dalits and weaker sections.”
Azad, backing Owaisi, said several people who criticise the AIMIM chief are often seen seeking his guidance in Parliament. He added that he was prepared to sacrifice every drop of blood to protect the Constitution.
Referring to the changing nature of political leadership, Azad said there was a time when people believed a king’s son would become king, but leadership now emerged from among the people. “I don’t know what a king is, but I am a true guard of the people and am here to serve them.”
Azad and Owaisi also reiterated their pitch for political empowerment through voting, saying the alliance wanted to build independent leadership for marginalised communities rather than depend on established political parties.
(Edited by Gitanjali Das)
